articles.title: Hate your blaring alarm? We found the best sunrise clocks for a gentler wake-up
articles.summary: Sunrise alarm clocks use light to wake you up gradually in the morning. Shop expert-recommended sunrise clocks from top brands like Hatch, Philips, Casper and more.
articles.body: If you start your day before sunrise, or if you’re looking for a more peaceful alternative to a blaring alarm clock, a sunrise clock may be your new favorite nightstand accessory. It mimics the natural sunrise by gradually lighting up at a certain time, and many even have gentle sounds to help you wake up. Best of all, it won’t jolt you awake like a normal alarm clock (or your phone) would. Using an alarm clock that simulates both the sunset and sunrise can help you fall asleep faster and wake up quicker in the morning, says Dr. Shelby Harris, a licensed clinical psychologist and the director of NY Sleep and Psychology. If you’re ready to make the switch, I consulted sleep experts on the benefits of sunrise alarm clocks and what to look for when shopping for one. I also pulled together a list of options to shop based on their guidance. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. Best sunrise alarm clocks Best overall The Hatch Restore 3 is a favorite among our experts and the NBC Selected team. “I’m more likely to sleep through the night now since I’m not anticipating being startled awake by my phone’s blaring alarm,” says NBC Selected reporter Zoe Malin. “The gradual increase of light in my bedroom lets me slowly transition from a deep sleep into consciousness.” You can use this sunrise clock to gently wake you up in the morning, moving from red to orange to white before your alarm sounds, or as a bedside light to wind down. You can also customize your sleep and wake up routine, play sound, adjust light and more using the companion Hatch Sleep app, or you can press the buttons directly on the device to control your nighttime or morning routine (keep in mind, you’ll need Wi-Fi connection for the device to work). It’s also a stylish alternative to other alarm clocks: “Since the curved device has a sleek, minimalistic appearance, it practically blends into my bedroom,” says Malin. There are a few differences between the Hatch Restore 2 and the Restore 3. “In terms of user experience, one of the biggest upgrades compared to previous models is the big button on the top, which lets me turn off my alarm, as well as turn on and off my sound machine, without using my phone once I program everything in the app,” says Malin. “That means I can keep my phone out of my bedroom overnight so I don’t get distracted by it.” Best app-enabled This Philips sunrise clock comes recommended by Dr. W. Christopher Winter, a neurologist and sleep specialist based in Charlottesville, Virginia. It has an auto-dimming display and five adjustable colors. The light gradually gets brighter and starts 30 minutes before your scheduled alarm time — the simulation starts off as a soft red and moves to orange and ultimately a bright yellow light to wake you up. The brand’s companion app, SleepMapper, lets you customize your chosen sunset and sunrise times, track your sleep over time and sync your sleep metrics with Apple and Google Health. Best portable Casper’s The Glow Light lacks sound options, so it’s less of an alarm clock and more of a sunrise- and sunset-simulating light. I use the Glow Light every day to wake up in the morning since the light gradually increases over the course of an hour based on the time I set on the companion app. It also functions as a bedside lamp: I usually use its auto-dimming feature to help me wind down at night, and the light will automatically turn off after an hour, so I can fall asleep without having to worry about it staying on. I like that the light has several straightforward, easy-to-use functions: You can twist it on its base to control its brightness, flip it upside down to turn it on and off, and lift it off its base to light up the way to a midnight snack (it’s durable enough to survive everyday tumbles, too). Best budget pick This Jall sunrise alarm clock has seven colored lights and 20 brightness levels to gradually wake you up over the span of 10, 20 and 30 minutes. It also has access to FM radio and seven built-in sounds to help you wake up or wind down, such as birds chirping, ocean waves and piano music. To better customize your routine, the clock also has 16 volume levels to choose from. Best customizable This Lumie sunrise clock lets you customize the maximum brightness and wake up gradually over anywhere from 15 minutes to 90 minutes. It also has a built-in alarm that lets you wake up with the radio or one of 15 sleep sounds to complement the light, according to Lumie. Plus, It has an auto-dimming display and a snooze button. Lumie also offers other, pared down Bodyclock models available: The Bodyclock Rise 100 loses its radio function and alarm while the Bodyclock Glow 150 includes 10 waking sounds and a duration of 20 minutes, 30 minutes and 45 minutes. Best sunrise clock and lamp combo Though this is a pricier option, I recommend pairing Loftie’s smart lamp and alarm clock for a complete sunrise clock and sound machine set. The lamp, which doubles as a chic piece of home decor, gradually brightens at the time you set via the companion app, while the alarm clock (which the brand notes is not a sunrise clock, but rather more like a sound machine) has sleep, meditation and wake-up sounds to help you rise in the morning and wind down at night. The lamp doesn’t display time nor has built-in sleep sounds like most other options on this list, so pairing it with the clock provides most of the capabilities you might be looking for in a new morning alarm. You can also set a sleep schedule on the app, which lets you gently transition from day to night by gradually turning down the brightness. How I picked the best sunrise alarm clocks To pull together our list, the experts recommended I keep the following key features in mind (more on these features below): Adjustable brightness and colors: Look for a sunrise clock that lets you adjust its brightness level and color options, whether via an app or manually on the device, for a more customizable wake-up and wind-down experience, experts say. Most sunrise clocks will also automatically adjust the light in the morning to mimic the gradual sunrise.Brightness level: You’ll sometimes see a sunrise clock’s brightness level expressed in lux or lumens: Lumens are a measure of brightness, whereas lux is a measure of lumens spread over an area, expressed in square meters. As you shop for a sunrise alarm clock, keep in mind that a higher lux signifies a more intense light. Most sunrise clocks I list below range between 100 to upwards of 300 lux.Sleep and wake sounds: Sunrise clocks can include sleep sounds that can either help lull you to sleep or gently wake you up in the morning — these typically range from nature sounds like birds chirping and ocean waves to white noise that reduces distractions. Some options only emit wake-up sounds if you haven’t turned off the light alarm after a certain amount of time, which can be a helpful backup plan, says Winter. Connected apps: Look for a sunrise clock with Wi-Fi or Bluetooth connectivity that lets you customize features like brightness level, sleep sounds, your wake-up schedule and more through a companion app, experts say. How do sunrise alarm clocks work? Most sunrise alarm clocks are fairly similar: They have a light that simulates the sunrise and sunset, which can gently increase and dim light without the adrenaline rush of a regular alarm clock. “They are especially beneficial during the winter when the sun rises later, and can help improve symptoms of seasonal affective disorder, insomnia, jet-lag and other sleep issues,” says Harris. Most sunrise clocks will start gradually brightening about 30 minutes to an hour before your scheduled wake up time (some give you the option to adjust that length via an app) to give you enough time to fully wake up at your preferred time. Can sunrise alarm clocks actually improve sleep? Sunrise clocks aim to help you wake up by lighting up your space gradually and slowly in order to give your body time to react and adjust, says Khosla. It’s a great, natural way for people who typically wake up before the sun is out, like those who work a night shift or parents waking up their kids before school, says Winter. “They mimic the look of a gentle sunrise, and light is a very powerful cue for helping with darkness at night for sleep and light in the morning for awakening our circadian rhythm,” says Harris. The presence (or lack) of light can be a main factor in regulating our sleep cycle: A 2019 study shows that light exposure too late in the day and too early in the morning may reduce your quality of sleep and affect the body’s circadian rhythm, an internal mechanism that regulates various processes within any given day or 24-hour cycle (including the sleep-wake cycle). They are a great alternative to traditional alarms, experts say. Disrupting your sleep too abruptly, such as with a blaring alarm clock, can push you to have lower sleep quality in the long run and can even affect your overall well-being, including weight gain, mood swings, lack of alertness and memory loss, says Khosla. How to shop for a sunrise alarm clock To determine the best sunrise alarm clock for your needs, my experts highlight a few key features to keep in mind when shopping for one, including brightness level and sleep sounds. Brightness level Brightness level plays a huge role in how you wake up (and whether you wake up on time) with a sunrise alarm clock. It may seem intuitive, but the brightness level of any sunrise clock is only accurate at a certain distance, so if you have it all the way across the room, it may not seem too bright and might not work as well, experts say. There are other variables, like the size of your room and your wall paint colors, that can impact how you perceive a light source, too. While sunrise alarm clocks available don’t generally have extremely bright lights, they can still be helpful. “You have to take what’s available commercially, recognizing that it may not be ideal,” says Dr. Seema Khosla, medical director at the North Dakota Center for Sleep. Your goal should be to sleep better, not necessarily to completely optimize the process, she says. Sleep and wake sounds In addition to mimicking a sunset that helps you slowly fall asleep to a dimming light, some sunrise alarm clocks also offer sleep sounds like white noise and nature sounds to help you fall asleep at night (the latter can also be used as a gentle alarm in the morning), says Harris. White noise in particular can accomplish multiple things, including reducing outside distractions and tapping into a calming reflex, experts told us in our guide to white noise machines. Connected apps “Sunrise alarm clocks that allow you to control and set them from your phone are the most convenient,” says Harris. Though options that don’t offer a Bluetooth feature or Wi-Fi connectivity are still just as effective (especially if you’re not necessarily tech-savvy, says Winter), most app-controlled clocks can offer the benefit of managing its brightness, setting a timer and browsing sounds to help optimize your bedtime and wake-up routine. Meet our sleep experts At NBC Selected, we work with experts who have specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also take steps to ensure that all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and with no undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Dr. Shelby Harris is a licensed clinical psychologist and the director of NY Sleep and Psychology in White Plains, New York.Dr. W. Christopher Winter is a neurologist and sleep specialist based in Charlottesville, Virginia.Dr. Seema Khosla is the medical director of the North Dakota Center for Sleep and a medical advisor for MedBridge Healthcare. Why trust NBC Selected? I’m a commerce editor at NBC Selected who has covered home, sleep and beauty for over five years. For this article, I spoke to three sleep experts about the benefits of using a sunrise alarm clock and whether they can actually improve your sleep. I also compiled expert recommendations, along with top picks tested by NBC Selected staffers. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

The two occupants escaped unhurt. The incident occurred close to an underground Metro construction site near Tidel Park.The white car was travelling along OMR near Thiruvanmiyur MRTS when a portion of the road near the median suddenly caved in, trapping one of its front tyres. A video showed an MTC bus attempting to squeeze past the car and a Metro barricade, after which the car plunged into the sinkhole and landed upside down.Work is under way to remove the car and fill the sinkhole. Chennai Metro Rail Limited (CMRL) officials are yet to confirm whether the underground Metro work is linked to the road collapse. articles.title: Stephen Hawking lived in a Victorian villa on this Cambridge site and wrote A Brief History of Time there; the house was later replaced by a building named after him
articles.summary: Stephen Hawking spent an important period of his life at a Victorian villa at 5 West Road, Cambridge, a property owned by Gonville & Caius College.
articles.body: Stephen Hawking spent an important period of his life at a Victorian villa at 5 West Road, Cambridge, a property owned by Gonville & Caius College. Hawking and his first wife, Jane, moved there with their children in 1975, after the stairs at their previous home became increasingly difficult for him to manage as his motor neurone disease progressed. Caius adapted the property for wheelchair access, allowing him to continue his academic work while raising his family. The house also became the place where he wrote A Brief History of Time, the 1988 book that introduced complex ideas about cosmology to millions of readers. Years later, the villa was demolished and replaced by the Stephen Hawking Building, creating a lasting physical connection between the Cambridge site and his scientific legacy.Stephen Hawking moved to the West Road villa in 1975Hawking and Jane had bought a townhouse in Cambridge in the late 1960s, but the stairs became increasingly difficult for him to manage as his condition progressed. In 1975, the family moved to 5 West Road, a house owned by Gonville & Caius College. The college adapted the Victorian property for Hawking's wheelchair, providing what Caius described as “lateral living”. Its large garden also gave their three children, Robert, Lucy and Timothy, space to play. The house allowed Hawking to balance family life with his demanding academic career. By then, he already had a strong connection with Caius. He became a Fellow in 1965, a year after receiving his PhD, and remained associated with the college for more than five decades.The house became the place where A Brief History of Time was writtenThe connection between the house and Hawking's most famous book comes directly from the physicist himself. In a 2015 speech at Gonville & Caius marking 50 years as a Fellow, Hawking recalled the property and said that he had written A Brief History of Time there. Published in 1988, the book explored some of the biggest questions in modern physics, including the origins of the universe, the nature of time, black holes and the laws governing the cosmos. Hawking presented these ideas for readers without specialist knowledge, using accessible explanations to explore how scientists had developed theories about the universe and its origins. The book became an international bestseller. Gonville & Caius says it eventually sold around 20 million copies worldwide, making Hawking one of the most recognisable science writers of his generation.Caius adapted its buildings around himThe changes to Hawking's home were part of a broader effort by Gonville & Caius to ensure that he could remain involved in college life. The college installed a lift and adapted its historic buildings so that Hawking could attend meetings, dine in Hall and take part in college activities. These changes enabled him to remain an active member of the academic community as his physical condition deteriorated. With that support, Hawking continued his research and writing while maintaining his connection with the college and its students and Fellows.A medical crisis changed how he communicatedIn 1985, Hawking developed severe pneumonia while in Switzerland. His condition became critical, and doctors asked Jane whether life support should be withdrawn. Caius arranged and funded a specially chartered flight to bring him back to Cambridge, where he was treated at Addenbrooke's Hospital. He underwent a tracheotomy and lost his natural speaking voice as a result. Hawking subsequently relied on computer-assisted technology and a speech synthesiser to communicate. Although the change fundamentally altered the way he interacted with others, he continued his research, writing and public work for decades.The Victorian villa was replacedThe house at 5 West Road eventually made way for a new college accommodation building. Gonville & Caius named the structure the Stephen Hawking Building, preserving the physicist's connection with the site. The redevelopment took place while Hawking was still alive. In February 2005, he cut the first sod to mark the beginning of construction. A foundation stone was unveiled later that year, and the building was completed in 2007. The redevelopment transformed the site from a private family residence into part of the college's accommodation facilities while retaining its connection with one of Caius's most celebrated Fellows.The building has 75 undergraduate roomsThe Stephen Hawking Building now forms part of Gonville & Caius College's accommodation. According to the college, it contains 75 undergraduate rooms, along with eight Fellows' sets and three supervision rooms. The project cost more than £10 million and received donations from more than 2,000 Caians, parents and friends of the college. The building also has a distinctive S-shaped design. Its unusual form was influenced by mature trees on the site that planners wanted to preserve, requiring the architects to shape the structure around them.The site preserves an unusual part of Hawking's legacyHawking died in 2018, aged 76, after more than five decades as a member of Gonville & Caius. The Victorian villa where he lived with his family no longer stands, but the site remains closely connected with his life. He lived there during a crucial period of his career, wrote A Brief History of Time there and later watched construction begin on the building that would carry his name.The story of 5 West Road brings together the personal and intellectual sides of Hawking's life. It was a family home adapted to accommodate his disability, the place where he wrote one of the most influential popular science books of the 20th century, and eventually the site of a permanent tribute to his contribution to science.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: A shopper paid C$5 for a small painting at an Ontario landfill donation centre, then spotted David Bowie’s name on the back; after experts authenticated the 1997 work, it sold at auction for C$108,120
articles.summary: Sometimes a bargain buy can turn out to be something far more valuable than it first appears.
articles.body: Sometimes a bargain buy can turn out to be something far more valuable than it first appears. That happened when a shopper picked up a small painting for just C$5 at a donation centre near a landfill in South River, Ontario. The surprise came after the buyer noticed the name David Bowie on the back. According to Cowley Abbott, the auction house that later handled the work, the painting was identified as DHead XLVI, a 1997 acrylic and computer collage on canvas. After its authenticity was confirmed, the painting went to auction in June 2021 and sold for C$108,120, including the buyer’s premium.From a donation centre to an auction roomThe painting had been sitting among unwanted household goods at a donation centre associated with the Machar Township landfill near South River. The shopper spotted the small canvas among the discarded goods and bought it for C$5. The painting measured only 9.75 by 8 inches, making its eventual price even more striking. On the back was a label identifying the artist as David Bowie, along with his signature and the date 1997.At first, however, there was no reason to assume the label was genuine. The circumstances of the discovery were unusual enough to make the buyer question whether the painting could really be Bowie's work. That is where the auction house's research began.Experts traced the painting to BowieCowley Abbott investigated the artwork before putting it up for sale. The auction house contacted David Bowie specialist Andy Peters, who helped confirm that the work was authentic. Cowley Abbott's own listing credits Peters with assisting in the authentication. The research also connected the painting to Bowie's work from the 1990s. Titled DHead XLVI, the piece is an acrylic and computer collage on canvas, signed and dated 1997 on the reverse. It belongs to Bowie's Dead Heads, also known as D Head, series.Bowie produced the series between 1995 and 1997. The works featured portraits of people from his circle, including friends, acquaintances and band members, along with some self-portraits. The individual paintings were identified using Roman numerals rather than conventional names. The sitter in DHead XLVI was not identified, adding another small mystery to the unusual artwork.Bowie was also a visual artistDavid Bowie is best remembered as a musician and performer, but his interest in art began long before the painting ended up at the Ontario donation centre. He studied art and design as a young man and remained interested in visual art throughout his life. He collected artwork and also produced paintings of his own.His work was influenced by modernist and expressionist artists, including Francis Bacon and painters associated with the London School. The Dead Heads paintings reflect that interest, using loose, energetic portraits rather than the polished appearance one might expect from conventional celebrity artwork. That background also helped explain why the small canvas could command serious interest once its connection to Bowie was established.The auction estimate was far lowerEven after authentication, Cowley Abbott did not initially put an enormous estimate on the painting. The auction house valued DHead XLVI at C$9,000 to C$12,000 before the sale. The online auction ran from June 15 to June 24, 2021. Interest quickly went beyond those expectations.Collectors from Canada and other parts of the world competed for the work, and the final price climbed to C$108,120, including the buyer's premium. That was nearly 10 times the high end of the original estimate. The sale also established a new auction record for an artwork by Bowie at the time.Why the story attracted so much attentionThe painting itself was rare, but its journey added another layer to the sale. There was the famous name, the limited number of works in the Dead Heads series and the fact that Bowie artwork rarely appeared at auction. Then there was the extraordinary story of how this particular piece had been found. It had gone from a landfill donation centre, where someone paid only C$5 for it, to an international art auction where collectors were prepared to spend more than C$100,000.The painting's path also shows how easily valuable objects can be overlooked when their history is unknown. Had the buyer not noticed Bowie's name on the back, DHead XLVI might have remained an ordinary-looking second-hand painting. Instead, the small canvas became one of the more memorable art discoveries of 2021, turning a C$5 purchase into a C$108,120 auction sale.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Malaysia bets on AI boom with 2,300-acre Silicon Island
articles.summary: Malaysia is reclaiming 2,300 acres of sea near Penang to build a new semiconductor hub as rising demand driven by the artificial intelligence boom pushes
articles.body: Malaysia is reclaiming 2,300 acres of sea near Penang to build a new semiconductor hub as rising demand driven by the artificial intelligence boom pushes the island’s existing industrial clusters towards their land limits.The Silicon Island project is expected to attract about 75 billion ringgit in investment, contribute 1.1 trillion ringgit ($269 billion) to Malaysia’s economic output through 2050 and create around 220,000 jobs, Bloomberg reported, citing a Deloitte study used by the project's developers.Penang has spent more than five decades building a major electronics and semiconductor hub, with companies including Intel, AMD and ASE Technology operating around Bayan Lepas. The state accounts for about 5 percent of global semiconductor exports, according to the state government.Silicon Island is intended to provide space for further expansion while helping Malaysia move beyond traditional chip assembly and testing into higher-value activities such as semiconductor design, advanced packaging and automated testing.The project comes as the global AI boom drives demand across the semiconductor supply chain. Malaysia is also benefiting as companies diversify production amid US-China tensions. Silicon Island has already drawn interest from local and international firms, particularly from Taiwan and Japan.READ ALSO: 'Targeting civilian infrastructure unacceptable': India condemns Houthis attack on Riyadh airportsAt its centre will be a roughly 700-acre Green Tech Park targeting semiconductor design, advanced packaging and automated testing. Its first phase is planned to operate entirely on renewable energy, according to the developers.However, the project will take years to complete. Reclamation could take three to four years, with the first industrial operations expected by early 2029 and the wider development potentially taking up to 15 years.Gamuda is financing the project's 14 billion ringgit reclamation and infrastructure costs through a syndicated loan, according to Bloomberg. The first industrial land sales are planned for early 2027.The island will also include around 20,000 homes, commercial facilities and green spaces. A 29.67-km Mutiara Line light-rail system is planned to connect it with Bayan Lepas, Penang International Airport and George Town, with operations scheduled to begin by the end of 2031.Silicon Island faces competition from Singapore, Vietnam and India, while higher land costs could make it less attractive to lower-margin manufacturers. Its developers are betting that Penang’s existing semiconductor ecosystem and growing AI-driven demand, rather than residential development, will drive the project’s success.You use AI every day. articles.title: Jon Stewart and his wife Tracey paid $4 million for a historic 45-acre New Jersey farm in 2016; the property now grows crops and cares for rescued cows, sheep, goats, pigs and chickens through their sanctuary foundation
articles.summary: Jon Stewart’s life away from television has included an unusual investment in New Jersey’s agricultural landscape.
articles.body: Jon Stewart’s life away from television has included an unusual investment in New Jersey’s agricultural landscape. In 2016, the comedian and his wife, Tracey Stewart, bought the historic 45-acre Hockhockson Farm in Colts Neck for $4 million. According to The Two River Times, which reported the purchase based on property records and local planning documents, the couple intended to turn the site into a working farm and sanctuary-education centre. Today, the property is known for both its agricultural use and its role in caring for rescued farm animals.A historic Colts Neck propertyHockhockson Farm sits along Route 537 in Colts Neck, between Laird Road and Swimming River Road. The property has a long agricultural history, with the farm dating to around 1780. When the Stewarts purchased it, the site included a farmhouse, two smaller houses, barns, other farm buildings, horse corrals and a farm stand.The property had also remained connected to the same family for generations. According to The Two River Times, members of the Cooke family had owned the farm for a couple of hundred years before it was acquired by the Stewarts’ entity, FSP LLC, also known as JTS Land Trust. The $4 million transaction was recorded on September 16, 2016. The purchase was part of the Stewarts’ plan to continue using the land as a farm while giving it another purpose centred on animal welfare and education.From working farm to animal sanctuaryBefore completing the purchase, Jon and Tracey Stewart had already outlined plans for a working farm and sanctuary-education centre. Their proposal involved working with Farm Sanctuary, a New York State-based organisation focused on rescuing and caring for farm animals. Plans included raising and selling crops, protecting rescued animals and creating opportunities for visitors to learn about farming and healthy eating.The project also involved plans for educational facilities. The couple had proposed an approximately 8,400-square-foot, two-storey education and visitor centre, along with other improvements to the property. The intention was to combine agriculture, animal protection and public education rather than simply preserve the land as a private estate. The proposal went through local agricultural and planning processes. In May 2016, the Monmouth County Agriculture Development Board approved the farm-related application, after which the project was to proceed to the township Planning Board for site-plan approval.What the farm is like todayThe property has continued to be associated with both farming and animal care. A 2024 report by 94.3 The Point described the Colts Neck property as a farm and animal sanctuary where crops are grown and rescued animals are cared for. The animals mentioned include cows, sheep, goats, pigs and chickens, giving the property the character of a traditional farm while also serving as a refuge for animals that need care.The farm is also substantial in its physical layout. According to 94.3 The Point, Hockhockson Farm includes two two-bedroom cottages, a pond, a pool and an equine facility with an arena. The property also has six barns, 16 stalls, five pastures, five paddocks, a five-car garage and a farm stand area. These features reflect the property's agricultural roots, with open land and farm infrastructure forming a significant part of the estate rather than the focus being solely on the main house.Tracey Stewart’s role in animal welfareThe sanctuary aspect of the property also connects closely with Tracey Stewart’s longstanding interest in animal welfare. According to The Two River Times, she was an animal advocate and former veterinary technician who had grown up on a farm. That background helps explain why the couple's plans for Hockhockson Farm went beyond conventional farming. The property was envisioned as a place where agricultural activity could exist alongside animal rescue and education.The Stewarts have consequently turned a historic New Jersey farm into a property with several overlapping roles. It remains tied to its agricultural past through crop production and farm infrastructure, while its sanctuary function gives rescued animals a safe place to live.A different kind of celebrity propertyFor a celebrity-owned property, Hockhockson Farm is notable for being shaped by a purpose beyond luxury. Its 45 acres bring together a historic farm, crop cultivation and an animal sanctuary, carrying forward the vision the Stewarts had when they acquired the property in 2016.The $4 million purchase has since taken on a distinctive character, with farming and animal welfare becoming two defining parts of the New Jersey property.You use AI every day. articles.title: Birmingham council sold a £395,000 house in 2013; 11 years later, it discovered a primary school had accidentally gone with it; now it is going to court to get it back
articles.summary: Birmingham City Council sold a three-bedroom former caretaker's house at auction in 2013 for £395,000, and a paperwork error meant the sale also
articles.body: Birmingham City Council sold a three-bedroom former caretaker's house at auction in 2013 for £395,000, and a paperwork error meant the sale also transferred ownership of George Dixon Primary School in Edgbaston. The mistake went unnoticed for 11 years while the school carried on as normal. It came to light on 12 April 2024, when the school looked into becoming an academy and learned that the council no longer owned the site. The council has since launched High Court proceedings in London against NH Care Ltd, the care provider that bought the house, and Lloyds Bank, its lender.A Birmingham house sale that came with a schoolThe house, on Fountain Road, was originally built for the school's caretaker, and its back garden borders the school's playing fields. It was bought at auction by NH Care Ltd, a company linked to businessman Sukhjit Bains, 50. Both the house and the school were registered under the same Land Registry title, which became the root of the problem when the sale paperwork was drawn up.The transfer was drafted on a TR1, the form used to transfer an entire registered title, rather than a TP1, which transfers only part of one. Because the house and school shared a title, the TR1 handed over both. According to the council, the form was prepared on behalf of the buyer, yet the council's own conveyancer signed it off without spotting the error.The buyer was a company, not Bains personallyAlthough Bains is the businessman most often named in coverage, the purchaser was NH Care Ltd. Bains and the company's two other directors are reported to have been unaware that the school had been included until the council contacted them. NH Care has reportedly not yet filed a response to the claim.After spotting the error, the council approached the company to resolve the matter. The council says Bains initially agreed to return the school, but that communication then stopped and the necessary paperwork was never signed. With no resolution, it turned to the courts.The case in the High CourtThe council is asking the court to correct the register and restore its ownership of the school. By its account, the original contract covered only the house, so the transfer document did not reflect what was agreed. It also argues the mistake was mutual, since the incorrect form was drafted by the buyer's lawyers and executed by the council's conveyancer. Finally, it says that selling school land and playing fields requires the consent of the Secretary of State, which was never obtained. A council spokesman said it is "pursuing the appropriate legal process to rectify the position."The school stays openGeorge Dixon Primary School, which has around 324 pupils, has continued to operate throughout. The house, meanwhile, has reportedly stood empty since the sale.The case lands as the council, which effectively declared itself bankrupt in September 2023, works through a large programme of property disposals. A sale that was meant to dispose of a former caretaker's house instead produced a dispute over a primary school, and a High Court claim to unwind it more than a decade later.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pakistan bets on electric vehicles as Middle East war sends petrol prices soaring 54%
articles.summary: Pakistan expects to achieve its electric-vehicle adoption target ahead of schedule as surging oil prices make the shift away from petrol-powered vehicles
articles.body: Pakistan expects to achieve its electric-vehicle adoption target ahead of schedule as surging oil prices make the shift away from petrol-powered vehicles increasingly attractive, a senior government official said.The government aims for electric vehicles to account for 30% of new vehicle sales by 2030 under its EV policy announced last year. Haroon Akhtar, adviser to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on industries and production, said the sharp rise in fuel prices has reduced the time needed for buyers to recover the higher upfront cost of EVs.“I feel that the target we had set in our electric-vehicle policy last year, we will achieve it much earlier as rise in oil prices has brought cost recovery of EV to one to one and a half year,” Akhtar told Bloomberg in Islamabad.“People are realizing the benefit now. You don't have to pay for petrol,” he said.Petrol and diesel prices in Pakistan have risen 54% and 43%, respectively, since the Middle East conflict began in February, according to data available from Pakistan State Oil Company Ltd.EV sales accelerate amid fuel price pressureAkhtar said sales of electric motorcycles and scooters have tripled from a year earlier, while electric-car sales have doubled, although industry-wide EV sales data is not publicly available.“This is an impact of the Middle East conflict, as fuel prices have gone up,” Akhtar said.Despite the growing incentive to switch to EVs, factors including high vehicle costs and limited charging infrastructure mean a large-scale transformation of Pakistan’s vehicle fleet and oil consumption will take years.The government is also preparing a new auto policy that could be presented to the cabinet within the next two weeks. It is considering tax incentives for EVs to narrow the price gap between electric and conventional vehicles, Akhtar said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: The skies have changed, so has IAF's mission: 94 years of India's air power
articles.summary: The Indian Air Force was raised on October 8, 1932, on the recommendation of the Skeen Committee, which had been set up to look into demands for the
articles.body: The Indian Air Force was raised on October 8, 1932, on the recommendation of the Skeen Committee, which had been set up to look into demands for the Indianisation of the Army. Its first squadron, the Tigers, came a few months later on April 1, 1933, at Drigh Road in Karachi, with four Westland Wapiti biplanes and five Indian pilots, a sixth having been moved to a logistics role. One of those five, Subroto Mukherjee, went on to become the first Indian chief of the air force. Born on October 8, the IAF is also the eighth oldest air arm in the world, behind those of the UK (1918), Italy and New Zealand (both 1923), Romania and Afghanistan (both 1924), Finland (1928) and Chile (1930).The air force todayIn the 94 years since, the IAF has grown into the world's fourth-largest air force by overall strength and a key component of national defence. It operates a diverse fleet of fighters, transport aircraft, helicopters, trainers and surveillance platforms. The fighter fleet includes the Su-30MKI, Rafale, Tejas, Mirage 2000 and MiG-29, while the C-17 Globemaster III, C-130J Super Hercules and C-295 handle transport and support. The force also flies Apache attack helicopters, Chinook heavy-lift helicopters and indigenous Dhruv helicopters.The big challenge for the force is numbers. The IAF currently has around 29 fighter squadrons against an all time high of 42, with each squadron typically comprising 16 to 18 aircraft. To bridge the gap, it is inducting Tejas Mk1A fighters, upgrading existing aircraft and adding advanced air-to-air missiles, unmanned systems and better air-defence networks. The government has also cleared the proposed acquisition of 114 Rafale fighters, subject to the procurement process. The priority is to strengthen squadron numbers, improve operational readiness and enhance indigenous aerospace capabilities, while the force continues to play a vital role in air defence, strategic deterrence, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief.A history in combatThe IAF has been in action almost since its inception. Its first operations came in the North-West Frontier Province from 1936 to 1947, followed by service alongside allied forces in the Second World War, notably in the Burma theatre. After independence, it flew into action in the First Kashmir War of 1947-48, airlifting troops and supplies into the Valley as well as air-to-ground operations. In 1962 it was in the background during the India-China war lifting men and material to the frontlines. The IAF played a much more active role in the 1965 and 1971 wars with Pakistan.Since 1984, Operation Meghdoot established India's presence on the Siachen Glacier, where IAF helicopters and transport aircraft remain the lifeline of troops at extreme altitude. The force supported the Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) in Sri Lanka between 1987 and 1990, and in 1999 carried out Operation Safed Sagar during the Kargil War. The 2019 Balakot air strikes and the aerial engagement that followed marked the first use of air power across the border for the IAF since the 1971 war. The IAF demonstrated its combat capability during Operation Sindoor, during which the force grounded the Pakistani Air Force with precision strikes and a solid air defence, ensuring that Islamabad sues for peace.As the Indian Air Force marks its 94th raising day, the country's air arm is working to ensure that both the capacity and effectiveness multiplies. The IAF is striving to remain in sync with the changing technologies to remain at the cutting edge as the nature of warfare changes. The air force is always ready to execute any task in war and peace that the nation entrusts upon us.IAF: A networked forceToday, the IAF is changing from a force built around individual platforms into a networked aerospace power. At the centre of that change is the Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) the digital backbone of India's air defence. Developed largely with Bharat Electronics Limited, it pulls data from ground-based radars, mobile surveillance systems, AWACS and AEW&C aircraft, surface-to-air missile networks and air traffic control into a single real-time picture. Commanders no longer work with scattered sensor feeds but with one recognised air picture that allows quick detection, identification, tracking and engagement of threats.The practical and operational gain here is of speed, IACCS shortens the time between a sensor picking up a threat and a shooter acting on it, which matters against cruise missiles, drones and precision-guided munitions, where reaction time is measured in seconds. It is backed by the Air Force Network (AFNET) a secure communications grid linking air bases, command centres and radar stations. Together, the two allow integration with the layered air defence systems of the other services.Unmanned systems extending the reachUnmanned systems are the second pillar of this transformation. Drones are no longer confined to surveillance and now handle intelligence gathering, precision strikes, electronic warfare, communications relay and battle damage assessment. The IAF's unmanned journey began with Israeli-origin Searcher and Heron UAVs and extended to Harop loitering munitions, with MQ-9B remotely piloted aircraft planned. Its roadmap covers propulsion, sensors, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare and autonomous mission execution, with the aim of building an indigenous ecosystem rather than simply buying drones. Importantly, they are not treated as a separate arm of warfare but integrated with fighters, surveillance assets and missile networks, acting as sensors, shooters and information nodes within the larger network.Bridges of friendshipThe force's strategic reach is best seen in its overseas engagements. Long-range airlifters such as the C-17 and C-130J, along with aerial refuelling, now let the IAF deploy across continents. It has taken part in Red Flag in the United States, Cope India with the US Air Force, Garuda with France and Indradhanush with the Royal Air Force. The most significant recent addition is Exercise Tarang Shakti, India's largest multinational air exercise, being held at Jodhpur with nearly 40 air forces.Beyond its military value, Tarang Shakti is an exercise in air diplomacy, showing that India can host and coordinate large-scale multinational air operations. Integrating several foreign contingents, planning complex missions and sustaining intensive flying require organisational capacity that few air forces possess. Exercises have become tools of strategic signalling and partnership-building as much as training.First responder: A friend in need is a friend indeedThe IAF has long been India's first responder at home, from the Gujarat earthquake and the 2004 tsunami to the Uttarakhand and Kerala floods, where helicopters and transport aircraft delivered supplies, evacuated civilians and restored connectivity. Over time, that mission has become part of foreign policy. After the 2015 earthquake in Nepal, Operation Maitri saw the IAF airlift rescue teams, engineers, medical staff and relief supplies. Operation Dost followed the 2023 earthquakes in Türkiye, with C-17s carrying NDRF teams, field hospitals and supplies, and Operation Brahma followed the March 2025 earthquake in Myanmar.The most striking recent example came in June with Operation Amistad, after twin earthquakes struck northern Venezuela. Two C-17s flew from Delhi to Caracas, covering more than 14,000 km in about 23 hours with 66 tonnes of aid, including an Army field hospital, over 35 tonnes of relief supplies and medical equipment, and two BHISHM Cubes, along with a 41-member team. The field hospital later began round-the-clock free medical services in Caracas. The mission took India's disaster response into Latin America and showed what the heavy-lift fleet can do. The IAF has also supported evacuations of Indian citizens from Yemen, Libya, Afghanistan and South Sudan.The measure of air powerAir power is now measured not only by the ability to fight and win wars, but by how well a force connects sensors to shooters, works with partners and responds when a crisis strikes. On all counts, the IAF is becoming one of India's most important instruments of national power, even as it works to rebuild its squadron strength.

articles.title: Stun grenades, shattered jaw, severed hand: France's student protests put police under scrutiny
articles.summary: France’s crackdown on high school protests is coming under growing scrutiny after several teenagers suffered severe, potentially life-changing injuries
articles.body: France’s crackdown on high school protests is coming under growing scrutiny after several teenagers suffered severe, potentially life-changing injuries during clashes with police.Thousands have also been arrested during the demonstrations aimed at demanding better-funded and better-equipped schools.A 14-year-old boy, identified as Eden, suffered a shattered jaw and severe dental injuries after a police tear gas grenade struck him in the face during the protest. His mother said he underwent surgery and is currently unable to speak or eat normally, relying on a straw for liquids.The police officer who fired the grenade was taken into custody a week later and faces a preliminary charge of violence by a public official resulting in mutilation or permanent disability, an offence punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Prosecutors said his use of the weapon appeared disproportionate. The officer told investigators he had acted within “a fraction of a second” to protect a female colleague who had exchanged blows with the teenager.Eden’s case is one of several serious injuries suffered by teenagers during the nationwide protests. In Lens, a 15-year-old lost a hand in an incident involving a police stun grenade. In Tours, prosecutors said a police riot-control round was suspected of causing the partial blinding of a 16-year-old.The injuries have intensified questions over the use of force against a movement made up largely of schoolchildren. Critics and human rights campaigners say police have responded disproportionately, while the government maintains that officers have intervened when demonstrations have turned violent, involving rioting, vandalism and attacks.Thousands arrestedThe protests began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September and have since spread across France, with students demanding increased funding and more replacement teachers.More than 6,500 people, mostly young protesters, have been arrested since the movement began, according to the Interior Ministry. Some 488 people were detained during nationwide demonstrations on Tuesday.Lawyers and researchers who study French policing warn that the scale of the crackdown could have consequences beyond the current protests, potentially leaving young people disillusioned with the French Republic and its ideals of “Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.”Alexis Baudelin, a Paris lawyer representing more than a dozen young protesters, told news agency AP that many of his clients were experiencing a protest and police custody for the first time.“It politicises you at an incredible speed,” he said, describing their arrests as a crash course in what he called “unrestrained violence from the police.”Baudelin said his clients had described spending hours in unsanitary cells, being unable to sleep and facing threats from officers during questioning.Government suspends some grenadesThe growing backlash prompted interior minister Laurent Nunez to suspend the use of the model of stun grenade suspected of causing the Lens teenager’s injury during high school protests.Nunez said there was a “strong possibility” that the weapon was involved in the teenager losing his hand and said authorities needed to establish exactly what happened.At the same time, he defended the police response in “almost all cases” as proportionate, saying officers had been forced to intervene when protests descended into violence.But he acknowledged that dealing with schoolchildren required a different approach.“You don’t handle a high schoolers’ movement in the same way as one by adults,” Nunez told broadcaster RTL.The government is also facing accusations of racial profiling. Three Paris-region teenagers who spoke to AP said they were arrested, handcuffed, searched and held in custody before being released without criminal charges.Two of them, both 17, said they believed they had been targeted because of their race. Warkya and another teenager are Black, while Samy described himself as Arab. French officials have repeatedly denied racism within the police, with prime minister Sebastien Lecornu calling such allegations “lies”.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Psychology says high-IQ people may not hurt more, but they can spend far longer analysing why they are hurting
articles.summary: Negative emotions do not spare people simply because they are intelligent.
articles.body: Negative emotions do not spare people simply because they are intelligent. Rejection can hurt, criticism can sting and heartbreak can leave anyone replaying old conversations at midnight. Having a high IQ does not make someone immune to anger, sadness, embarrassment or disappointment. But there may be a difference in what happens after the initial emotion appears.Research suggests that cognitive ability, particularly verbal intelligence, can be linked to the way people process difficult experiences. One study published in Personality and Individual Differences found that verbal intelligence was a unique positive predictor of worry and rumination, while non-verbal intelligence showed a different relationship with post-event processing. The study involved 126 undergraduate participants, so its findings should not be treated as proof that every highly intelligent person overthinks. The more interesting question, then, may not be whether intelligent people feel more. It may be whether their minds have more ways of thinking about what they feel.The emotion may be ordinary, but the analysis can keep goingImagine someone receives unexpectedly harsh criticism from their manager. The first reaction is familiar: embarrassment, anger or disappointment. But instead of leaving the incident there, the person may begin examining every detail. Why did the manager use that tone? Was the criticism really about the missed deadline? Did something from last month's meeting contribute to it? Was the comment fair? What did the manager actually mean? One thought can quickly become several.This is where intelligence and rumination can sometimes overlap. The Penney study found that higher verbal intelligence predicted greater severity of worry and rumination, although the relationship was not the same across all measures of intelligence. That distinction matters. It does not mean that intelligent people are destined to overthink, or that rumination is a sign of intelligence. It means that certain cognitive abilities may give a person more mental material with which to examine an unpleasant experience.A strong verbal ability, for example, can make it easier to remember exactly what was said, construct alternative explanations and imagine what could have happened differently. That can sometimes be useful. A person might eventually realise that a friend's angry reaction was influenced by stress at work. They may recognise that a relationship had been struggling for months rather than ending suddenly. They may notice a pattern in their own behaviour that they had previously missed. In those cases, reflection can help turn an emotional reaction into understanding.When reflection becomes ruminationThe problem begins when thinking stops producing new understanding. A person can know exactly why a friendship ended and still replay the final conversation. They can understand why their partner left and still reread old messages. They can recognise that their boss was under pressure and still spend another hour wondering whether one particular sentence sounded insulting. Psychologist Ethan Kross of the University of Michigan describes this kind of repetitive negative thinking as “chatter”. His research focuses on how our inner voice can help us solve problems but can also become a negative thought loop that makes it harder to think clearly and regulate emotions.Kross has explained that introspection can be useful, but it can also backfire when people become narrowly focused on the most negative parts of an experience. Instead of gaining perspective, they become increasingly absorbed in the problem. That is an important difference between reflection and rumination. Reflection asks, “What can I learn from this?” Rumination keeps asking, “Why did this happen?” without necessarily moving towards an answer. For someone with a highly active analytical mind, recognising that difference can be particularly important. The ability to generate another explanation does not necessarily mean another explanation is needed.Intelligence does not automatically come with emotional wisdomBeing good at solving intellectual problems does not guarantee that someone will know what to do with a difficult emotion. A person may be capable of analysing a breakup from ten different perspectives and still not know whether they need rest, reassurance, a conversation or simply time to grieve. That is because understanding an event intellectually and regulating the emotions surrounding it are different abilities. Research also does not support the simplistic idea that high IQ automatically means greater emotional intensity. In one study examining objective IQ alongside emotional measures, affect intensity did not significantly differ with IQ in the sample.So the more accurate picture is not that highly intelligent people experience sadness, anger or rejection in some completely different way. The emotion itself can be perfectly ordinary. What may differ for some people is what their mind does next. It may search for patterns, replay conversations, construct explanations and examine every possible interpretation.Sometimes that extra processing helps a person understand what happened and move forward. Sometimes it simply keeps the emotional experience alive. The useful skill, therefore, may not be learning how to analyse more. It may be learning when analysis has already done its job. Because a sharp mind can find answers in difficult experiences. But it can also find one more question long after the answer is already there.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: From 19 Hawai Sepoys and 4 aircraft to Rafales and Sukhois: The IAF's 94-year journey
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Four Westland Wapiti biplanes, six RAF-trained officers and 19 Hawai Sepoys.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Four Westland Wapiti biplanes, six RAF-trained officers and 19 Hawai Sepoys. That was the Indian Air Force in 1933, when its first operational flight took off from Drigh Road in Karachi, then part of British India.The Wapiti was a far cry from the fighter jets of today. A two-seater biplane, it reflected the modest beginnings of a force that would go on to fight wars, defend India's skies and carry out missions far beyond the country's borders.More than nine decades later, the IAF operates Rafales, Su-30MKIs, Mirage-2000s, MiG-29s, Jaguars and Tejas, supported by transport aircraft, attack and heavy-lift helicopters, drones and a layered air-defence network. In 2025, it put many of those capabilities to work during Operation Sindoor.The distance between those four Wapitis and today's fighter fleet is not simply a measure of technological progress. It is also a record of the wars India fought, the lessons it learnt and the kind of air force it gradually decided it needed.As the IAF completes 94 years on October 8, its journey tells the story of how each conflict, each new aircraft and each technological advance helped shape the force it is today.1932–1945: Six officers, 19 Hawai Sepoys and a world warThe IAF was established on October 8, 1932. Its first operational flight followed six months later, on April 1, 1933.Six RAF-trained officers and 19 Hawai Sepoys made up the small unit at Karachi's Drigh Road. The four Wapiti IIA aircraft formed the nucleus of what would eventually become No. 1 Squadron.The early years were far removed from the era of precision weapons and network-centric warfare. In 1936, the fledgling force saw its first operational action from Miran Shah in North Waziristan, now part of Pakistan, supporting Army operations against insurgent Bhittani tribesmen of Pashtun origin near what is today the Pakistan-Afghanistan border.More aircraft and personnel followed. A second flight was raised in April 1936 and a third in June 1938, bringing No. 1 Squadron to full strength. When World War II began, it was still the only IAF formation, with 16 officers and 662 men.Then the war changed the pace of everything.India, then under British rule and part of the Allied war effort during World War II, saw the creation of Coastal Defence Flights to protect key ports and coastal installations.These flights were based in several strategically important coastal cities across the subcontinent: Madras, Bombay, Calcutta, Karachi and Cochin, with another later established at Visakhapatnam.The aircraft and roles also began changing as the demands on the force grew.By 1941, the IAF had begun moving away from the Wapiti. Tiger Moths were being used for elementary training, while No. 1 Squadron moved to the Westland Lysander. No. 2 and No. 3 Squadrons operated the Audax before the Hurricane entered the picture.By the end of 1942, the IAF was operating five squadrons. In 1943, No. 7 Squadron moved to the US-built Vengeance dive bomber. By the end of 1944, nine squadrons were active, most flying Hurricanes and one flying Spitfires.The growth was rapid. By 1946, the force had around 28,500 personnel, including about 1,600 officers. Twenty-two Distinguished Flying Crosses and several other decorations had been awarded to its personnel during the war.In March 1945, the force received the prefix "Royal".That prefix, however, would not last long.1947–1962: Partition, rebuilding and the arrival of jetsIndependence in 1947 brought freedom, but also a sudden reorganisation of the military.The division of assets meant the IAF lost personnel and equipment to the newly formed Royal Pakistan Air Force. Its strength was nearly halved. Several units were disbanded or transferred, while the remaining force had to reorganise even as the Kashmir conflict began.There was little time for a clean transition.The IAF continued expanding its capabilities during the conflict. Spitfires and Tempests were used, a photo reconnaissance flight was formed and plans were made to rebuild B-24 Liberators from salvaged aircraft.In January 1950, India became a republic. The word "Royal" disappeared from the force's name.The IAF at the time had six fighter squadrons, flying a mix of Spitfires, Vampires and Tempests. There were also bomber, transport, observation and communications elements. Pilot training was being expanded through dedicated flying training schools.The jet age was already beginning to change the force.The Vampire brought jet fighters into the fleet. The Ouragan arrived in 1953. Then came the Mystere IVA, Hunter and Canberra. The IAF's planned strength was expanded from 15 squadrons towards a 33-squadron force.The 1961 UN mission in Congo gave the Canberras a chance to operate far from India's borders. At home, however, the security environment was changing quickly.In 1962, India signed protocols with the Soviet Union for the acquisition of MiG-21 fighters and surface-to-air missiles.The Soviet-made aircraft would go on to become one of the most recognisable names in Indian military aviation.1965–1971: MiG-21s, Gnats and a changing balance of air powerThe years after the 1965 India-Pakistan war brought another round of modernisation, coming soon after the setback of the 1962 war with China and amid then-Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri's efforts to strengthen the armed forces.MiG-21FLs began replacing older aircraft, while the Gnat, which had performed well during the 1965 war, returned to production. By 1968, four more Gnat squadrons had been formed.The Su-7BM also joined the IAF fleet.The IAF was no longer simply adding aircraft. It was building a system around them.Older equipment was phased out while MiG-21s, Su-7s and HF-24s increased in numbers. The air defence Ground Environment System was being planned to improve surveillance and response, while the Air Force Academy at Dundigal was inaugurated in January 1971.Then came December 1971.The IAF flew thousands of sorties during the war and secured air superiority in the eastern theatre during the Bangladesh Liberation War.Gnats and MiG-21s became central to the fighting. The war demonstrated what a much larger and better-equipped IAF could do compared with the force that had entered the Kashmir conflict two decades earlier.India's military dominance eventually forced Pakistan to accept one of the largest surrenders in military history.The fleet continued to change after the war. Jaguars and Mirage 2000s joined the inventory, adding new capabilities to an increasingly varied fighter fleet.That variety would become one of the defining characteristics of the IAF.1999: How Kargil changed the use of air powerThen came the Kargil conflict in 1999 posing a very different problem.There was no conventional air war in the traditional sense. Indian aircraft had to operate over some of the world's highest and most difficult terrain, while avoiding crossing the Line of Control.Operation Safed Sagar became one of the IAF's most closely watched operations. Mirage-2000s carried out precision attacks, while MiG aircraft provided additional strike and support.Operation Safed Sagar provided a major boost to the forces on the ground.Mi-17 helicopters were also used in the operation.The experience showed the importance of accurate navigation, intelligence, precision weapons and the ability to operate at high altitude. Official figures released by the government later put the IAF's Kargil effort at around 5,000 strike missions, about 350 reconnaissance and electronic intelligence missions and roughly 800 escort sorties, apart from more than 2,000 helicopter sorties.The Mirage-2000, in particular, acquired a new reputation during the conflict after being used for precision attacks against key positions.The lessons from Kargil did not end with the guns falling silent.From parade ground to the frontline: Women in IAFAnother important chapter in the IAF’s journey has been the growing role of women in the force.Women officers began joining the IAF in the early 1990s, initially in ground duties before moving into transport aircraft and helicopters. In 2016, Avani Chaturvedi, Bhawana Kanth and Mohana Singh became the first three women fighter pilots.The journey continued with Shivangi Singh becoming India’s first woman Rafale pilot, while Bhawana Kanth became the first woman IAF officer to qualify as a Fighter Combat Leader in 2026.During Operation Sindoor, Wing Commander Vyomika Singh emerged as a prominent face of the IAF, briefing the nation alongside Colonel Sofiya Qureshi.From ground duties to fighter cockpits and frontline operations, women have steadily expanded their role. On Air Force Day 2026, their leading drill sequences and marching contingents marked another step in that journey.2016 onwards: Tejas and the push for an Indian fighterFor much of its history, the IAF had relied on aircraft designed and built abroad — British, French, Soviet and later Russian, American and other European platforms.The Tejas changed that equation.The indigenous Light Combat Aircraft was designed as a multi-role fighter with digital avionics, fly-by-wire controls and extensive use of composite materials. The first Tejas squadron was inducted into the IAF in 2016.It was not an overnight replacement for the established fighter fleet. The IAF continued operating its Su-30MKIs, Mirage-2000s, MiG-29s and Jaguars even as Tejas numbers grew.The more recent Tejas Mk1A represents another step. In September 2025, the defence ministry signed a Rs 62,370-crore contract with HAL for 97 aircraft, 68 fighters and 29 twin-seaters.The aircraft are to have more than 64% indigenous content and incorporate systems including the UTTAM AESA radar. Deliveries under this contract are scheduled to begin in 2027-28.However, the programme has also faced delays. The IAF is still awaiting deliveries under an earlier order for 83 Tejas Mk1A aircraft, highlighting the challenge of converting indigenous manufacturing plans into operational strength.That is significant for another reason. The Tejas programme is increasingly about building an Indian aerospace manufacturing base, rather than simply producing one aircraft.Rafale, Su-30MKI and a very different fighter fleetThe other side of the modernisation story is the arrival of advanced foreign-origin platforms.The Rafale brought a new level of multi-role capability. The Su-30MKI became the IAF's heavy fighter workhorse. Mirage-2000s and MiG-29s remained important parts of the combat fleet, while Jaguars continued to perform strike roles.The fighter fleet is only one part of the picture.The IAF's transport arm has grown around aircraft such as the C-17 and C-130J. Apache and Chinook helicopters have added attack and heavy-lift capabilities. The C-295 is gradually replacing the older Avro transport fleet.The C-295 programme is also an important marker of how India's approach to military aviation is changing. Sixteen aircraft are to be delivered from Spain, while 40 are being manufactured at the Tata-Airbus facility in Vadodara.So the modern IAF is not just about fighter jets flying faster and carrying more weapons. It is about getting troops and equipment into difficult areas, moving supplies, watching the battlefield, protecting air bases and keeping an air picture running across hundreds of kilometres.2025: Operation Sindoor and the new face of warfareOn May 7, 2025, the IAF found itself in a conflict very different from the air battles of 1965 or 1971.Operation Sindoor was launched after the Pahalgam terror attack.India said nine terror infrastructure sites in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir were targeted in the opening strikes. The PM Modi-led government described the action as "focused and measured", with the initial statement saying no Pakistani military facilities had been targeted.The operation subsequently widened.Pakistan launched drones and missiles towards Indian military targets. India's response involved a layered air-defence network. Akash systems operated alongside legacy systems such as Pechora and OSA-AK, while the Integrated Air Command and Control System helped bring information and responses together.The significance of Sindoor lay partly in what was happening behind the aircraft seen in the sky.Radars, command centres, air-defence systems, drones, electronic warfare, missiles and fighters were all part of the same operational picture. The government later said the IAF's IACCS worked alongside the Army's Akashteer and the Navy's Trigun to provide a common real-time picture during the operation.The IAF also carried out strikes against Pakistani military targets later in the operation.The counterterror operation hit 11 Pakistan airbases, including strategically crucial Nur Khan airbase near its capital Islamabad and Sargodha airbase.According to Indian government accounts, Indian aircraft hit airbases and command-and-control infrastructure, while Indian air-defence systems countered Pakistani missile and drone attacks.It was a reminder that modern air warfare is increasingly about networks as much as aircraft.A fighter may deliver the weapon, but the information that tells it where to go can come from a much larger web of sensors, satellites, radars, intelligence platforms and command systems.Beyond the battlefield: The IAF that rescues and evacuatesThere is another side to the IAF that rarely gets the same attention as fighter aircraft.Transport aircraft and helicopters have repeatedly been used in disaster relief, evacuation and humanitarian missions. From flood rescue and earthquake relief to evacuating Indians from conflict zones abroad, airlift has become a routine part of the force's job.That role was also highlighted in the IAF's 2026 Vayushakti exercise, which featured not only fighters but C-17s, C-130Js, C-295s, helicopters and remotely piloted aircraft. The exercise included scenarios involving airlift, rescue and evacuation alongside combat missions.It is a very different job from sending a fighter on a strike mission, but it depends on the same thing: Getting an aircraft, crew and equipment where they are needed, quickly.At 94, the next challenge awaitsThe IAF is now looking at a future in which the fighter fleet will have to work alongside drones, loitering munitions, long-range missiles, electronic warfare systems and increasingly sophisticated air-defence networks.The government has also cleared the next steps for the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft, or AMCA. In May 2025, the AMCA programme execution model was approved with industry participation, allowing Indian private and public-sector companies to bid independently or as joint ventures or consortia for development of the prototype.There is also another Rafale requirement in the pipeline. In February 2026, the Defence Acquisition Council gave an Acceptance of Necessity for Multi Role Fighter Aircraft, identified as Rafale, along with combat missiles and an airborne high-altitude pseudo-satellite system. The government said the majority of the MRFA aircraft would be manufactured in India.The direction is clear even if the final shape of the fleet will take years to emerge.From four Wapitis in 1933 to today's Rafales, Tejas and advanced air-defence systems, the Indian Air Force has come a long way.Its journey has been shaped by wars, the lessons learnt from them and decades of technological progress. What began with a handful of officers and Hawai Sepoys has grown into a modern air force with capabilities extending far beyond those of its early years.Ninety-four years after its first flight, the IAF continues to grow and adapt, just as it has through every major chapter of its history.

articles.title: NSW and Australian governments buy 74,000-hectare outback station, protecting state’s first pink lakes and habitat for 70+ threatened species, including brolga, pink cockatoo and slender darling pea
articles.summary: Pink lakes within the New South Wales national parks estate will be protected for the first time after the NSW and Australian governments jointly
articles.body: Pink lakes within the New South Wales national parks estate will be protected for the first time after the NSW and Australian governments jointly purchased Pulgamurtie Station, a 74,000-hectare property about 235 kilometres north-east of Broken Hill. This landscape is home to more than 70 threatened species, including the iconic brolga, pink cockatoo and slender darling pea.Two lakes, plenty of skyPink lakes are rare in NSW, and many appear only in certain seasons. The two on Pulgamurtie are among the state's most spectacular natural wonders. Their peculiar hues occur naturally due to the presence of certain microorganisms, including algae and bacteria, that thrive in highly salty water and produce pink pigments.The station covers more than 74,000 hectares. Beyond the lakes, it has sweeping outback plains, rolling sand dunes and thriving wetlands. The larger lakes and wetlands are critical feeding and breeding grounds for thousands of waterbirds, including some migratory species that travel between Australia, Russia, China and Japan.NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe said the purchase is a rare chance to protect the natural environment and its threatened biodiversity. “These will be the first pink lakes protected by the NSW national park estate. This is a once-in-a-generation conservation and tourism opportunity that will protect these spectacular landscapes and allow more people to experience them,” the minister said. “Few places capture the scale and diversity of the NSW outback quite like Pulgamurtie, where a mosaic of wetlands, lakes and rolling arid plains exists side by side. This is a critical investment in conservation that will help safeguard this unique landscape, its wildlife and its rich cultural heritage for generations to come.”Brolga and the pink cockatoo call this homeThis property is home to more than 70 threatened species, including the brolga, the pink cockatoo and the slender darling pea. This effort is part of a push to protect landscapes that are under-represented in the reserve system. The two governments are jointly buying high-priority conservation properties through the Australian Bushland Program. The federal government says such purchases have helped it protect more than 25% of Australia's land mass.Federal Environment Minister Murray Watt said protecting the habitat is the current focus. “Australians love spending time in the bush and this purchase will protect more of it for future generations. With our natural environment under significant pressure, the Albanese Government is committed to protecting and restoring more land across Australia,” the minister said. “Through our partnership with the NSW Government, we’re helping secure important habitat and expand the network of protected areas in places that deliver the greatest conservation benefits. By protecting and conserving diverse areas of NSW, we’re supporting many threatened species and the habitats they call home.”Aboriginal cultural heritagePulgamurtie is not only known for its natural environment but also for its Aboriginal cultural heritage. The property is a significant part of Dreaming songlines and has historic stone artefacts, hearths and grinding stones.Moving ahead, the NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) will work closely with the Malyangapa Aboriginal Community, neighbouring landholders and other stakeholders.Mark Sutton, a representative member of the Malyangapa Native Title Board, also expressed hope about the purchase. “The Malyangapa people are supportive of the continued expansion of protected areas in Far West NSW. The acquisition of Pulgamurtie ensures that representative landscape types and Aboriginal cultural heritage will be protected,” he said. “We look forward to engaging with National Parks and Wildlife Services to create another recreational destination for locals and visitors alike.”Pulgamurtie was on the market for around two years. It was acquired after it failed to meet its reserve at a public auction. NPWS has bought five of the 60 properties sold in Far Western NSW in 2024 and 2025.Meanwhile, the NPWS will eventually consider the possibility of welcoming visitors. The station sits along the Silver City Highway, and NPWS will explore campsites near the larger lakes, day-use areas, walking trails and scenic drives. Birdwatching is on the list, along with views towards the Koonenberry Range. No opening date has been given. According to the government, national parks contribute $433 million a year to Western NSW and support nearly 9,000 jobs.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
