articles.title: Meet Advay Jain: Indian-American kid who made Guinness record as the youngest person to publish a book. He was 3 when he wrote 'Dino Learns Not To Waste Food'
articles.summary: An Indian-American toddler, Advay Jain, has made Guinness record as the youngest person (male) to have published a book.
articles.body: An Indian-American toddler, Advay Jain, has made Guinness record as the youngest person (male) to have published a book. He was 3 years and 345 days old when he published 'Dino Learns Not To Waste Food'. Now he is 4. Consul General of India in New York, Binaya Srikanta Pradhan, felicitated Jain at his office for his achievement and congratulated him. "Consul General @binaysrikant76 welcomed 4-year-old Indian-origin author Advay Jain @theauthorsiblings, Guinness World Record holder for being the youngest male to publish a book," the social media post from the consulate read."Through his book “Dino Learns Not to Waste Food”, Advay inspires young readers to value food and embrace the importance of avoiding food waste.""Warm congratulations to Advay on this remarkable achievement, and best wishes to Advay and his 12-year-old sister, Ms. Avya, also an author and painter, as they continue to inspire young minds through their creativity and stories," it added.Earlier in 2026, Jain, a pre-schooler from South Brunswick, New Jersey, published his book from Panda Publishing Agency. The story was inspired by Jain's transition to a new pre-school where he was not allowed to bring food from home. Jain's father Neeraj Kumar said more than 1,300 copies of the book were sold worldwide and the number was still growing.In an earlier interview cited by reports from South Brunswick, Neeraj Kumar said that he and his wife Sonal Bansal began the journey of making Dino's story into a book in July 2025 and the process took 10 months. Advay's elder sister Avya too is also a published author of 'The Call of the Nether'.Advay's storytelling started through images, as he used to draw his ideas on walls. His parents never stopped him but helped him culminate those into a fully developed book of drawings and little stories.The four-year-old is already working on a sequel where Dino will learn other important lessons.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cornell’s Jane Doe is ‘terrified’ after police swarmed her home in a swatting incident, her lawyer says
articles.summary: One month ago, the woman now known as Cornell’s Jane Doe was living in New York City and trying to break into the hotel industry, her lawyer says. Now she’s...
articles.body:
One month ago, the woman now known to America as Cornell's Jane Doe was living in New York City among thousands of other aspirational twentysomethings, attempting to break into the hotel industry and build a new life, according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra.

But that plan has been derailed since she filed a lawsuit against Cornell University and others, alleging she was raped at a frat house in 2024.

Instead, Giuffra said, Doe spent Wednesday taping up paper to obscure the windows of her parents' home out of fear that a gunman could attack her, and reeling from a swatting episode that he said prompted police to swarm their home Tuesday night with weapons drawn.

Doe is increasingly scared for her own safety, Giuffra said in a phone interview with CNN on Wednesday as he detailed his client's deteriorating mental state after an escalating series of violent threats.

Officers pointed weapons at Jane Doe's boyfriend, her brother and her father after receiving a bogus tip that "someone was killing people in the house" on Tuesday evening, he said.

Death threats, doxxing attempts and an outpouring of anger online have also been levied at his client, Giuffra added.

"I don't think she's in a good spot now," Giuffra said. "She's scared."

The public fallout from her allegations have rocked one of the country's leading educational institutions. The university, its campus police force and the Tompkins County District Attorney's office have each faced scrutiny over how they initially investigated her claims. Anger among students was palpable during a Wednesday sit-in on the Ithaca, New York, campus.

Doe herself has been following media reports and social media posts on her case, Giuffra told CNN as he described a family reeling from a sudden and terrifying ordeal that punctured their sense of safety.

"Before (this week), it was just a lunatic fringe, which you can be dismissive of," he said. "Now it's somebody taking real steps to harm you, and that's pretty frightening."

Doe's parents are furious after a fake tip to police, lawyer says

At 7 p.m. on Tuesday evening, a police officer in Doe's hometown was dispatched to respond to a disturbing call: A man had shot and killed his mother and then turned the gun on his sister.

The information was bogus. But the officer, believing an active-shooter situation was unfolding, rushed to Doe's home, where he saw a car backing out from the driveway, according to a police report from the incident obtained by CNN.

As he apprehended the two men in the vehicle – later revealed to be Doe's brother and her boyfriend – another figure emerged from the home's doorway. "I'm the dad. What's going on?" he yelled, according to the report. The man told police his daughter is Jane Doe of the Cornell case and that the family was "being threatened by numerous unknown people."

The swatting incident was an escalation in a series of threats to Doe's safety that have roiled her family this week. The term "swatting" refers to false tips made to law enforcement agencies with the intention of having armed officers deployed to somebody's home or place of business.

"Luckily the brother was in his car, (he) put his hands up," Giuffra told CNN on Wednesday, relaying the events of the night. "(Doe's) boyfriend got thrown on the ground," and her father also had "guns put in his face," according to Giuffra. "If you had a trigger-happy cop, or somebody had done the wrong thing, somebody could have ended up dead," he said.

Police are now investigating the swatting attempt, and the FBI is also looking into the events, according to Giuffra.

According to Doe's lawyer and two police reports reviewed by CNN, police arrived moments after Doe received a separate phone call from somebody claiming to share a first name with one of the seven men she named in her civil complaint.

According to her account to officers in the reports, Doe "began panicking" when she received the call, "because (her phone) wouldn't stop ringing." She informed officers about that previous call while they were at her house following the swatting tip.

Before the night was over, Giuffra's wife told him that she, too, had received a threatening phone call. "These people have done so much research into (Doe)," Giuffra said. It is not clear whether the separate threats cited in the police reports were connected.

Giuffra said he was in contact with Doe and her family on Wednesday. Her parents are angry and she is terrified, he said.

The lawyer shared with CNN an audio recording of a call he says was placed to his office on Wednesday afternoon. In the recording, a man identifies himself as "the person who called your client."

The man also is heard saying: "I'm telling you guys simply, I think you should advise your client to withdraw the case. Otherwise blood will be shed."

Doxxing attempts also have taken their toll

Tuesday's swatting attack was an escalation of the potential dangers facing Doe since she filed her lawsuit last month, but it was far from the only threat she's received, her lawyer said.

Giuffra estimated that dozens of threats have been made against her since mid-September, when his client filed a 101-page complaint alleging she had been sexually assaulted and raped by several members of the Xi chapter of Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity.

Doe's civil suit was filed against the university, the fraternity, seven fraternity members and others. It alleges that members of the frat drugged and sexually assaulted her in October 2024 and invited other fraternity members in a group chat to join the assault. The suit also alleges the school failed to protect her and adequately punish the accused students, who all deny wrongdoing.

Giuffra detailed to CNN another threat: a text message, sent to Doe's phone on Monday, with three emojis depicting guns.

Meanwhile, a handful of online personalities with large followings have led a campaign to uncover the identity of Doe, whose name was redacted in legal documents. One wrote on X to 347,000 followers in late September: "If you happen to know who this Cornell 'Jane Doe' is, get in touch and I would be happy to publish her name and identifying information."

He later claimed to have identified her and said he shared that identity online before deleting his post. Such behavior is known as doxxing, or sharing someone's personal information or identity online without their permission.

It has left Doe frightened and struggling to come to terms with the impact of the lawsuit, which has prompted outrage and scrutiny of how the university and its private police force initially investigated her claims.

On Wednesday, Doe was "taping paper over windows in the house she's lived at her whole life," Giuffra said, "so people can't see into her house to take a shot at her."

"I don't get shook up very easily, but this shook me up. I didn't want to have a body on my hands," he said.

"The dad is … concerned for his daughter. He can't believe this has happened out of something where she's just trying to stand up for herself and be heard," Giuffra added.

"But the parents are really strong people, and they're going to protect their daughter."

Doe had studied hotel administration at Cornell's prestigious Nolan School of Hotel Administration, and it had been her "dream" to attend the school, Giuffra said. Her complaint says she traveled across the country and arrived at the school with the same "hopes, expectations and trepidations of other high school graduates."

But she left the program without graduating after the alleged assault took place two years ago. Doe initially attempted to begin a career in New York City earlier this year, but after filing the lawsuit – "when everything hit the fan" – she instead returned to her family home, where she has been staying with her boyfriend, her lawyer said.

"The dream is lost," Giuffra told CNN, referring to her hopes of working in the hospitality industry.

Instead, Doe has been hiding out at her parents' home, where she has been following the intense media coverage of her case.

"It's kind of hard to switch it off," Giuffra said. "She comes from a generation of people who are focused on social media." CNN is not specifying the location of Doe's family home at her lawyer's request.

She has been going on walks but otherwise spends much of her time indoors. She remains in contact with some of the friends she made at Cornell, Giuffra said.

"She's a little paranoid," Giuffra said of his client. "If she's out of (the) safety zone of her family, she just doesn't seem to function well." A few friends of the family know she has returned home and have been providing support, and Doe's mother has taken time off from work to help look after her daughter, he said.

Doe is also aware of the many messages of support that she has received from around the world since filing the lawsuit, according to Giuffra.

Cornell, which recently appointed former acting US Attorney General Sally Yates to investigate the school's handling of sexual assault claims, was the site of a seven-hour sit-in on Wednesday to show "solidarity with Jane Doe," according to flyers for the event.

During a meeting with Cornell's Graduate and Professional Student Assembly on Monday, university President Michael Kotlikoff acknowledged the mounting frustration across campus as more details and questions emerge about Doe's 2024 allegations.

"We're all angry. I understand that anger," Kotlikoff said, according to the independent student newspaper the Cornell Daily Sun. "People want easy answers to this."

The school's president previously released a video statement promising further review of the case, saying it highlights "heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization, and aspects of party culture, alcohol, and drug use."

"The students up there (at Cornell) have been overwhelmingly supportive, and it's wonderful," Giuffra said. "They're trying to effect change, and bringing out to the light something that's been going on for generations."

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

articles.title: AI may raise homework scores but weaken actual learning, World Bank warns
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Better homework, worse exams.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Better homework, worse exams. International evidence cited by the World Bank suggests that unrestricted use of generative AI can improve what students submit while weakening what they actually learn — a warning with implications for countries such as India as AI use expands in classrooms.The World Development Report 2026 devotes a separate section to “Generative AI and the Erosion of Knowledge, Learning, and Human Skills”, cautioning that tools such as ChatGPT can reduce the mental effort through which reasoning, writing and knowledge are built. The report does not cite an India-specific study on student learning outcomes in this section.Its strongest evidence comes from China. A study covering students in Grades 7-12 found self-reported AI use rising from almost zero to around 80% between 2022 and 2025. Six months after first use, homework scores improved 18% even as students spent less time on assignments, while monthly in-class examination scores fell 20%. Students who had ever used AI also scored, on average, 5-7% lower in senior high-school and college entrance examinations. The report cautions that the study has not yet been peer-reviewed and reflects the early phase of AI adoption.Gaurav Nayyar, who led the World Bank team that prepared the report, said the evidence points to both opportunity and risk in education. “If students outsource the learning process to AI, then... that will be a problem,” he told TOI.He said the evidence so far appeared more encouraging when AI was used by teachers rather than directly by students. “There is much more benefit when AI is being used by teachers rather than by students,” Nayyar said, pointing to its use in personalising and customising instruction to suit different learners.Other research reviewed by the World Bank points in the same direction. Participants using large language models for research displayed lower cognitive effort and weaker reasoning, while studies found mental effort declining even when output quality improved. Students given unrestricted AI access also performed worse later when the technology was withdrawn.The report warns that if students use AI to complete homework, the “productive struggle” central to learning can disappear, potentially weakening foundational skills in reasoning and writing.But it does not argue against AI in education. A synthesis of experiments across China, Ghana, Nigeria, Türkiye and the US found that 30 sessions of AI-powered tutoring produced learning gains equivalent to at least 0.56 years of schooling, particularly when AI complemented teachers and included safeguards against shortcuts.“AI can augment human capabilities,” the report said, “but it must not replace the processes through which more advanced skills are acquired.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Israel-Britain ties hit new low as Jerusalem consulate loses its diplomatic status
articles.summary: The diplomatic relationship between Britain and Israel has suffered a fresh setback after Israel said the British Consulate in east Jerusalem would no
articles.body: The diplomatic relationship between Britain and Israel has suffered a fresh setback after Israel said the British Consulate in east Jerusalem would no longer function as a consulate, with 20 British diplomats, including the consul general, set to leave the country.Britain, however, said the building would remain open and continue to provide services, with a smaller diplomatic team working from the site. The move marks the latest deterioration in ties between the two long-standing allies.Britain to retain smaller diplomatic presenceIsraeli foreign minister Gideon Saar said the consulate would continue operating with a seven-member diplomatic “task force” and a “very limited” scope of activity.“Israel will no longer turn its cheek to diplomatic attacks against it," Saar said in a statement to news agency Reuters.The sign outside the consulate was removed, but British officials said the building would remain open. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said it would now “be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem” following discussions with the Israeli government.A small team of diplomats will continue working there, Miliband said.“This will ensure that we maintain our longstanding British presence and the U.K.’s role in support of a two-state solution,” he added.Britain had previously threatened to expel Israeli diplomats if Israel closed the consulate. articles.title: Girl's death prompts call for allergy management ratings
articles.summary: Mia St Hilaire had a tree nut allergy and suffered an anaphylactic shock after drinking a milkshake.
articles.body:
The family of a 12-year-old girl who died after drinking a milkshake made in an unwashed blender at a cafe have called for a dedicated rating that scores food businesses on their allergy management.

Mia St Hilaire, who had a tree nut allergy, suffered an anaphylactic shock and died after she drank a Twix milkshake at the Pop Inn Cafe in Bermondsey, south-east London, in August 2023.

Her order contained hazelnut residue because the blender had not been washed after a Kinder Bueno milkshake was made in it beforehand, an inquest concluded on Thursday.

In a statement, her family said "significant changes" were needed to protect people with food allergies.

In January 2025, the cafe was fined £18,000 and its proprietor Baris Yucel was given 100 hours of community service after admitting six criminal charges related to the Food Safety Act.

These included not making allergen advice available or visible to consumers, failing to manage allergen contamination during the food production process, and serving food that contained an allergenic ingredient that was not supposed to be present.

CCTV evidence showed that Yucel had not cleaned the blender before preparing Mia's milkshake.

Assistant coroner Briony Ballard listened to evidence at London Inner South Coroner's Court before publishing a narrative conclusion on Mia's death.

In a statement read after the conclusion of the inquest, Mia's parents Adrian St Hilaire and Chanel Spence said families with food allergies should not be "at risk" when eating out.

"We hope that lessons will be learned from Mia's death and that changes will be made to prevent other families enduring the devastation that we now have to live with," they said.

"Consumers rely on food hygiene ratings when deciding where it is safe to eat, but they do not tell us anything about the way a food business runs allergy management systems.

"There should be a separate, clearly displayed rating dedicated to the allergy management, like the food hygiene rating.

"This would mean that people with allergies could make more informed choices about where they eat."

Natasha's Foundation founder Tanya Ednan-Laperouse, whose daughter died aged 15 from an allergy to sesame in a Pret A Manger baguette, said allergies were "a serious, unpredictable medical condition".

"The inquest into Mia's death illustrates just how far we still have to go to improve awareness, understanding and regulation of food allergies," she said.

"Natasha's Foundation is working hard with business, schools, communities and the government to increase awareness and understanding of food allergies to try to prevent other families from having to go through the terrible loss that Mia's family endure."

Rebecca Sudworth, director of food policy at the Food Standards Agency, said her "deepest sympathies" were with Mia's family.

"Food businesses must take allergen risks seriously, every time," she said. "People have the right to know exactly what is in their food and drink, and it is a business's legal duty to provide accurate allergen information.

"We recently produced new guidance for businesses to make sure they understand their responsibilities to inform consumers about allergens, including the risk of cross-contact, and we are keeping this policy under review. We also have free allergy training and practical tools that businesses can use."

articles.title: Warrants used to search Andrew's homes were unlawful, court says
articles.summary: A criminal investigation into the former prince continues and police have retained material seized from his homes.
articles.body:
Thames Valley Police has accepted warrants it used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes at the time of his arrest in February were unlawful, the High Court has been told.

Following Thursday's hearing, items seized in the raid continue to be held by the police, with a further hearing to take place in 2027 to decide whether the material can be used as evidence.

Meanwhile, the criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing.

The former prince, who denies any wrongdoing, was arrested by police on 19 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after which he launched a legal challenge over the legality of the search warrants.

The force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the properties.

On Thursday at the High Court, judge Mr Justice Hilliard said Mountbatten-Windsor and the police had agreed that the search warrants had been unlawful.

However, he added: "The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful."

Mountbatten-Windsor opposes the police's bid to retain the evidence, the judge said, and another hearing is expected in 2027.

His lawyers have used a judicial review to challenge the actions of the force's chief constable and the Central Criminal Court in the build-up to his arrest.

His arrest arose after the US Department of Justice published documents which raised suspicions he had forwarded confidential information to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein when Mountbatten-Windsor was a UK trade envoy in 2010.

He has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.

The court heard on Thursday that Thames Valley Police seized documents and electronic devices when they raided Mountbatten-Windsor's homes earlier this year.

Thames Valley Police's position was that they had applied for search warrants under section eight and nine of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 at a hearing at the Central Criminal Court the day before the search.

That court determined that only section eight search warrants were needed and they were granted on that basis - but subsequently, a legal challenge has established that the court should have issued them under the section nine.

The judge explained on Thursday why the police could keep hold of the former prince's items that had been seized.

He said: "There would be little point in handing property back if it could then simply be lawfully seized under some other provision."

A Thames Valley Police spokesperson said: "The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgement on our ongoing investigation.

"We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout.

"We accept the position that the initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.

"Legal proceedings are currently ongoing to decide how material seized during the searches will be managed and whether we can lawfully retain it in support of our ongoing investigation."

The force said its "investigation into alleged misconduct in public office by a man in his 60s from Norfolk remains ongoing, and we continue to pursue all reasonable lines of enquiry to effectively and fairly progress this investigation".

Legal wrangle continues over material seized from former prince

The next stage in this legal dispute will be a behind-closed-doors hearing over whether the police can still retain material seized from Mountbatten-Windsor's homes under alternative powers designed for situations like this.

The error that has led to Thames Valley Police accepting the search warrants were unlawful relates to the particular power the judge permitted the force to use when its officers raided the properties.

Strict legal safeguards on searches bar the police from automatically seizing sensitive material without thinking through in advance the need to take it.

Examples of that material include advice from a suspect's lawyer or material which does not really belong to them, such as copies of confidential work-related papers from an employer.

In practice, if the police find such material during a search, they should return it rather than use it in their investigation.

The category of search warrant that was granted by the court in this instance did not take into account the possibility of such protected material being seized.

However, the law says police can in fact seize that kind of material - or potentially retain it in the event of an error - providing they pass some extra tests.

Thames Valley Police must now convince a judge that the material is likely to be of "substantial value" to their investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor and, ultimately, potential evidence to present to a court.

So while the force has conceded the search warrant was unlawful, a judge will have to decide whether this alternative search power, with its extra safeguards, justifies them keeping and using the material after all.

articles.title: Has Israel shut the UK consulate in East Jerusalem – or downgraded it?
articles.summary: British Foreign Secretary Miliband said the consulate building would remain but would be called ‘UK Mission, Jerusalem’.
articles.body:
The British government has said it will retain its presence in occupied East Jerusalem after Israel removed the signage of its consulate amid deteriorating diplomatic relations.

The removal of the signage comes as Israel announced that 20 British diplomats, including the consul general, would have to leave the country and return home.

Britain’s Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband, said on Thursday that the consulate building would remain but would be downgraded to the “UK Mission, Jerusalem”.

The Israeli government’s decision to close the consulate followed Miliband’s announcement last month that Britain would ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

What did Israel say about shutting the consulate?

In a post on X, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar reiterated on Thursday morning that “no action can be taken against Israel without Israel taking appropriate retaliatory measures”.

In retaliation for the sanctions on the occupied West Bank settlements, Saar outlined the four steps that Israel was taking against the UK, including:

Removal of British representatives from the International Assistance Centre for Gaza

Ending British activity to train Palestinian Authority forces in the occupied West Bank

Closing the British Consulate in Jerusalem

Prevention of entry into Israel of 12 elected officials and other British citizens involved in “anti-Semitic and anti-Israeli activity”

“We did not want to come to this, but the actions of the Labour government led us here,” Saar wrote, adding that the sanctions and the “hostile rhetoric” of ethnic cleansing of Palestinians had forced their hand against the British government.

“The British Consulate in Jerusalem ended its duties today. The Consul General and 20 diplomats are ending their duties and will leave Israel,” he said, adding that while the building is the property of the British government, Israel has allowed them to operate a task force of seven diplomats in the building with a “very limited scope of activity”.

The minister explained that the decision was also based on an understanding reached with the British government last night.

But isn’t the UK saying its mission will still function?

In a statement, Miliband said that the British government had been “clear” that it did not accept Israel’s decision to close its consulate, which has been around for nearly 200 years, reiterating its “longstanding view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.”

“The UK Mission, Jerusalem is independent, operational, and will continue to deliver vital services and our work with the Palestinian people.

“This will ensure that we maintain our longstanding British presence and the UK’s role in support of a two-state solution.

“Without an understanding, we would not have the necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises. Accordingly, the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security,” he said.

“We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence and we will not take reciprocal action while such discussions are underway and credible.”

“The UK stands steadfast by the measures we took on September 8 , in concert with the international community, in support of a two-state solution to deliver peace and security for the people of Israel and Palestine,” Miliband added.

Reports of reciprocal action against the consulate closure, including expelling one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat who had to leave the country, first came from the Israeli newspaper Ynet, citing a message sent to Israeli officials.

On the consulate’s closure, Stephen Doughty, Minister of State in the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, told BBC Radio on Thursday morning that the British government was continuing conversations with Israel about the issue.

“You can see what’s changed in terms of a name, but crucially a presence remains,” he said.

Asked about reports of a British threat to expel Israeli diplomats, the minister did not comment on it, but said they engaged with Israel in a “mature, responsible and practical debate”.

Reporting from London, Al Jazeera’s Camille Nedelec said the downgrading of the consulate marked “a low point in UK-Israeli relations”.

While a consulate mainly helps citizens, in this case British-Palestinian nationals, a mission usually refers to a diplomatic representative.

However, according to Vincent Fean, former British Consul General in Jerusalem, it did not “matter” what the consulate was now called.

“The Israeli electorate faces elections on October 27 and I think the plan of the British government is to wait and see what comes from those elections and to deal with whatever government the Israeli electorate chooses,” Fean told Al Jazeera.

“I think that the key point is that Ed Miliband acted correctly on September 8, specifically on the issue of E1 – the red line – settlement the Israelis are planning and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich says is designed to bury the two-state solution,” he added. The E1 settlement aims to link Ma’ale Adumim and other illegal Israeli settlements to occupied East Jerusalem, effectively severing the West Bank in two.

The British consulate first opened in 1839 but closed in 1914 at the start of the First World War. It was later re-established as a consulate-general in 1948 after the British Mandate in Palestine ended.

Relations soured following the new Labour government’s decision to impose sanctions on settlers and illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Miliband announced the measures and said last month that imports of all goods produced by illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank would be banned.

In his speech, he said there was “ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank – perpetrated by settler terrorists.”

“The sanctions regime will target illegal settlements and settlement expansion, not Israel,” he said.

“We will continue to support important and valued trade with Green Line Israel precisely because we support the two-state solution, including security and prosperity for Israel,” he added.

However, Israel condemned the announcement last month and called it a “series of anti-Israel decisions by the Labour Government”.

Saar said the “accusations made today by the Foreign Secretary of the Labour Government in the British Parliament were outrageous lies,” and set out the four reciprocal actions.

As the British consulate is in a part of Jerusalem that Israel captured in the 1967 war and has occupied ever since, it does not have the legal right to close the mission.

However, due to Israel’s ongoing occupation of the Palestinian territories, it practically decides what can function in East Jerusalem.

articles.title: Iran-backed Houthis expand attacks on Riyadh as Yemen war escalates
articles.summary: The leader of the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen has warned Saudi Arabia to prepare for a long conflict, as his group intensified its attacks on the kingdom — targeting its airports and military facilities for a third consecutive day.
articles.body: The leader of the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen has warned Saudi Arabia to prepare for a long conflict, as his group intensified its attacks on the kingdom — targeting its airports and military facilities for a third consecutive day. The group said Thursday it had carried out a new wave of attacks targeting two civilian airports — King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Najran Airport near the southern Saudi-Yemen border — and the Royal Saudi Air Force’s King Khalid Air Base. It claimed the attacks involved both cruise and ballistic missiles and had caused damage and disrupted air traffic. Images posted on X and verified by CNN showed smoke rising over Terminal 4 at King Khalid International Airport as well as what appeared to be a damaged Saudi aircraft, while the Associated Press cited a witness as saying several explosions had been heard in Riyadh, including at the airport. While Saudi authorities have not directly commented on whether the airports were attacked, they said Thursday they had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles fired toward Riyadh and that falling debris had damaged a kindergarten and a medical clinic. The US Mission in Saudi Arabia said it was “aware” of attacks targeting the airport in Riyadh and warned American citizens to exercise heightened vigilance, noting previous attacks on civilian airports in the country and cautioning the conflict “has the potential to escalate.” It warned of possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions, and said US government employees now required “special authorization” to use the airport and remained barred from traveling within 20 miles of the Yemen border. The news comes after three people were killed and 36 wounded over the past two days in Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport and Abha International Airport, near the Yemen border. Leader’s warning In a televised speech Thursday, Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi vowed to continue attacking Saudi targets and confronting Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. He warned Saudi Arabia against continuing its military campaign in Yemen, saying his group had the military capabilities and resolve to withstand a lengthy conflict. “The Yemeni people today possess all the determination and elements of strength, regardless of how long the war lasts,” al-Houthi said. The Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa, have been at war with Yemen’s internationally recognized government and a Saudi-led coalition since 2015. The conflict intensified in July after the collapse of the US-Iran ceasefire, with the Houthis expanding missile and drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities, airports and shipping routes. Saudi Arabia has responded with airstrikes and support for Yemeni government forces. In recent weeks, the Houthis have threatened to broaden the scope of their attacks within Saudi Arabia. In a statement Thursday, they warned employees, engineers and workers at Saudi oil facilities to avoid locations that could become targets of future attacks. The group also renewed previous warnings to airlines, airport operators, travelers and workers at Saudi airports and facilities. “The more the Saudi enemy persists in its aggression and blockade, the greater its losses become,” al-Houthi said. ‘Dawn of Yemen’ The latest escalation comes as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces continue Operation “Dawn of Yemen,” a major offensive aimed at reversing recent Houthi gains in Yemen. In recent weeks, fighting has intensified along Yemen’s western coast and around the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital shipping route connecting the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Yemeni government forces have claimed to have recaptured several positions near Bab al-Mandeb, Mocha and Dhubab, although the Houthis dispute those claims. On Thursday, Yemen’s internationally recognized government said its forces had carried out 1,729 precision strikes against Houthi targets during the offensive, claiming to have killed 1,370 fighters and destroyed or disabled 300 vehicles and other military assets. The same day, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of escalating its air campaign, claiming Saudi warplanes had carried out 59 airstrikes and missile attacks across Sanaa and several Yemeni provinces over the previous 24 hours, causing civilian casualties. CNN cannot independently verify either claim. However, the Houthis have dismissed reports of major battlefield losses, accusing regional media outlets of exaggerating advances made by Saudi-backed forces. Earlier this week, Houthi missiles landed near Aden International Airport, the main airport serving Yemen’s internationally recognized government, forcing the diversion of a commercial flight from Cairo, according to Yemeni government officials. The Saudi-led coalition said late Wednesday that it responded to that attack by launching a large-scale operation striking 82 Houthi military targets in Saada, Hodeidah, Al-Jawf and Marib provinces. According to the coalition, the targets included missile depots, command centers, communications facilities and weapons stockpiles.

images.caption: A member of Houthi security forces stands next to a poster of Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi at the site of a gathering of Houthi supporters to show solidarity with the movement as fighting intensifies across several fronts, in Sanaa, Yemen October 7, 2026.

articles.title: Ukraine’s migration challenge won’t end with a peace deal
articles.summary: For many Ukrainians, the question will not be whether they love their country or miss home; it will be whether returning makes sense for their family.
articles.body:
In 2022, millions of Ukrainians crossed the border carrying suitcases and hoping to return home within weeks or months. Four years later, many of them have built lives elsewhere.

That is why a peace agreement may end the war without ending Ukraine’s migration crisis.

Around 5.6 million Ukrainians remain abroad because of the full-scale war, according to the Center for Economic Strategy. More than 4.4 million people who fled Ukraine were under temporary protection in European Union countries as of July, according to Eurostat.

These numbers are not simply statistics about people waiting to go home. They represent millions of lives that have continued while the war has continued. Children have entered local schools. Parents have found jobs. Families have rented homes and built new social networks. Some have learned new languages and established careers. What began as temporary displacement has, for many, become an established life.

That does not mean Ukrainians no longer want to return. Research by the Center for Economic Strategy found that 43 percent of Ukrainian refugees plan to return to Ukraine, while 36 percent do not plan to return. Among those who intend to come back, nearly 80 percent say they would do so only after the war is definitively over, and security conditions improve.

The difference is important. For many Ukrainians, the question will not be whether they love their country or miss home; it will be whether returning makes sense for their family.

A mother may want to return, but her child may have spent four years in a foreign school and now speak the local language more confidently than Ukrainian. A parent may miss home but have a stable job abroad. A family may still own an apartment in Ukraine, but it may need major repairs — or no longer exist.

In 2022, returning home often meant going back to the life people had left behind. After several years abroad, it can mean starting over.

Time itself has become a migration factor. This is why the end of the war cannot be treated as an automatic solution to the refugee question. Peace is essential for return, but peace alone cannot recreate the lives people had before 2022. Housing, employment, schools, healthcare and security will all matter. So will something less tangible: whether people believe that their future is once again in Ukraine.

The most important group may be neither those who are certain they will return nor those who have decided to stay abroad. It may be the people who have not yet made up their minds. Their decision will be shaped by what Ukraine looks like when the war ends.

If they see safe communities, functioning schools, available housing and real employment opportunities, some may choose to come back. If they see uncertainty, destroyed housing and limited economic prospects, they may decide that the life they have built abroad is the more practical choice.

Ukraine also needs to prepare for another possibility: not everyone will return. That should not automatically be treated as a failure.

Ukrainians who remain abroad can still maintain strong connections with their country. They can send money to relatives, invest in Ukrainian businesses, return for visits, support communities and contribute professionally from abroad. Ukraine may emerge from the war not only with returnees, but with a much larger and more globally connected diaspora.

The government cannot order people home. Nor should it. It can, however, influence the conditions under which families make their decisions.

That means protecting property rights and providing credible compensation, expanding housing reconstruction and affordable rental and mortgage programs, creating jobs, supporting professional retraining and giving Ukrainians abroad reliable information about security, schools, healthcare and employment in their home communities.

The goal should not be to persuade every Ukrainian abroad to return. The goal should be to make returning a realistic choice.

For the United States and Ukraine’s European partners, this distinction matters. The future of Ukraine’s population will shape not only its recovery but also its economic strength, democratic resilience and long-term security.

Kateryna Odarchenko is president of the PolitA Institute for Democracy and Development, a political consultant, a partner of the SIC Group Ukraine and a member of the International Association of Political Consultants.

articles.title: ‘This is a crisis of hope’: Echoes of 1968 as France’s students rise up
articles.summary: As in 1968, when student protests triggered nationwide strikes, today’s crisis is about generational discontent.
articles.body:
The scale of protests raging across France over the education system, attracting hundreds of thousands of pupils, teachers and parents, has been described as exceptional by unions and student movement organisers.

“I think this is very historic and unprecedented by how big it is,” Alice Cohen-Morzadec, international spokesperson for France’s Student Union, said on Tuesday, when government sources put the number of protesters at 266,000.

“Some are saying this is the biggest movement since May 1968,” she added.

The student protests at Paris universities nearly five decades ago were initially driven by opposition to an outdated and overcrowded system, limited opportunities and broader political concerns.

The unrest soon spread beyond campuses, expanding into nationwide strikes involving millions of workers that virtually paralysed the country.

Back then, President Charles de Gaulle was in power. Today’s protests come as France heads into next year’s presidential elections, which are being eyed by the far right .

As in 1968, the protests that started on September 21 at an underdeveloped Paris suburban high school are about funding for education, teacher shortages, overcrowded classes, and school facilities.

But those are triggers and not the deeper causes, according to historians and student movement organisers.

“For the young people, this is a crisis of hope. You can see they are bombarded daily with economic problems, political extremes, dangers of warfare in Europe, the threat to their careers from AI, high youth unemployment rates, the climate crisis,” Andrew Smith, historian of modern France and lecturer in Liberal Arts at Queen Mary University of London, told Al Jazeera.

He said students are dissatisfied because of a lack of substantive interaction between the government and student representatives and unions in recent years.

“It has been difficult for the government to meet with interlocutors and try to have dialogue with social partners,” he said.

Robi Morder, a researcher on social movements in France, said the lack of communication reflects the current government’s approach.

“In 1990 and 1998, governments were led by socialists and leftists. Some of the ministers had been in the youth movement. So when there was an issue, the government knew how to negotiate. In 1990, the president himself received a delegation of students,” said Morder.

“We are not in the same situation because the government is not only from the other side politically, but they also don’t have the experience of the old political class,” he added. “They don’t know how to negotiate a social conflict. The government’s first answer is, ‘It is nothing; we will call the police, and everything will be OK.’”

Student organisers say they are frustrated because they feel the government is not taking them seriously.

“This is too much. Enough is enough. We have been making these demands for years. We need more money for education, we need more teachers, we need better facilities,” said Chloe Grunenwald, vice president of the Federation of the General Association of Students (FAGE), the largest organisation of its kind in France, representing some 300,000 students.

When interviewed by Al Jazeera , several students said they had joined recent protests in solidarity with those who first took to the streets. The broadening of the coalition is illustrated by the fact that both Grunenwald and Cohen-Morzadec represent university unions rallying in support of high school pupils.

Smith and Morder spoke of the differences between now and 1968.

“This school year started very differently. The never-ending heatwaves is one thing that really provoked it and made it catch fire. We had classrooms with over 40 people in temperatures exceeding 40 degrees [Celsius;104 Fahrenheit]. That is untenable,” Smith said.

Protest organisers and unions have also complained about what they see as police brutality.

“Unfortunately, the media are talking about how bins are being burnt, schools are being blocked, and how it is a form of violence. The real violence is actually coming from the government side,” said Cohen-Morzadec.

In a sign of conciliation, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Wednesday said, “Students must be heard,” while Interior Minister Laurent Nunez ordered police to suspend the use of stun grenades against protesting high school pupils.

But those moves might not be enough to calm the anger.

“We are going to mobilise until we get our demands, especially because we have October 17 and November 20 – as an international date for the youth in all Europe to mobilise for our future, so we want to continue at least until those dates, if not further,” said Cohen-Morzadec.

Nationwide strikes and antigovernment demonstrations are scheduled for October 17, expected to bring together a large number of unions to air their grievances against soaring energy and food prices, proposed budget cuts, and freezes on public sector salaries.

The strikes are backed by the left-wing France Unbowed (LFI) party, led by Jean-Luc Melenchon, and the country’s main labour union, known by its French acronym, CGT.

Critics have accused the LFI and Melenchon of inciting violence to score points against the government, an accusation they and protest organisers deny.

“Our message has been the same. We are fighting for our rights and our demonstrations are passive. We are not working on behalf of anyone else,” said Grunenwald.

Student unions have published a list of 10 demands they say will cost the government 1 billion euros ($1.1bn), and have promised to keep up the pressure until all those requirements are met.

Among the demands are calls for greater investment in schools and universities and more staff and space in higher education. Students are calling for stronger financial and housing support, affordable university meals, and an end to higher fees for international students. They also want an end to what they call “all forms of repression linked to the high school and student movement”.

images.caption: High school students protest against education conditions in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, France, October 1, 2026 [Firas Abdullah/EPA]

articles.title: Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while repairing campaign sign
articles.summary: Bernadette Greene-Placentia says her memory of the attack is spotty and that she was knocked unconscious.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains details which some readers may find distressing.

A congressional candidate in Arizona has said she was raped in a car park as she repaired campaign signs late at night in her district.

Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a Democrat, told the Phoenix New Times she was knocked unconscious during the alleged attack in the Phoenix suburb of Sun City on 14 August, waking up to find a man on top of her.

She said she did not initially notify police until filing a report with the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office two weeks later.

Her Republican opponent, Abraham Hamadeh, urged authorities in a statement to "investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place".

"No American should become a victim of a crime in their own community," said Hamadeh, who is running for a second term in office.

Greene-Placentia told the Phoenix New Times she was "embarrassed" and "just wanted to forget", but felt compelled stand up for other victims.

The candidate said she often speaks on the campaign trail about fighting for Arizonans.

She told the Phoenix New Times: "I didn't feel like I could keep saying that if I weren't also fighting for women that are victims of sexual assault."

The BBC has contacted the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office for comment. A sheriff's spokesman told the New York Times the investigation was ongoing.

After the attack, Greene-Placentia said she withdrew from the public for two days, staying in an apartment separate from her husband and skipping a campaign event.

When she emerged, her husband, campaign staff and others in her circle noticed she was acting differently, according to Phoenix New Times.

Greene-Placentia said she did not see a doctor following the alleged attack in congressional district eight and did not receive a sexual assault examination.

She said her memory of what happened was spotty and she did not get a good look at either of the two assailants, but described them as white men, according to the New York Times.

She told the Phoenix New Times that one assailant may have made a comment about her political affiliation, together with a misogynistic slur, although she could not be certain.

The candidate said she was concerned voters might think it was a political stunt to win points in a heavily Republican district. She also expressed concern that the allegations might overshadow her messaging around affordability.

articles.title: White House on possible Iran strikes before midterms: Trump ‘has all options’
articles.summary: President Trump has “all options” available concerning the next steps with Iran, amid reports the president is weighing whether to resume major combat operations before or after elections in the U.S. and Israel. “The Commander-in-Chief has all options available at any time. The United States is in a very strong position with control of the…
articles.body:
President Trump has “all options” available concerning the next steps with Iran , amid reports the president is weighing whether to resume major combat operations before or after elections in the U.S. and Israel.

“The Commander-in-Chief has all options available at any time. The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing,” a White House official told The Hill.

“Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways; the easy way or the hard way. President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States,” they added.

The U.S. and Iran are at an impasse more than seven months into the war. The Islamic Republic is deeply strained under a U.S. economic pressure campaign and naval blockade against its oil exports. But the regime has demonstrated its leverage against Trump by disrupting energy exports in the Strait of Hormuz and striking American targets and its allies across the region.

Trump has threatened Iran with an ultimatum to make a deal or risk annihilation. The president has asked the Pentagon to develop strike options against Iranian targets that could be exercised before the midterm elections, The Atlantic reported Wednesday.

While Trump has said the midterms and voters’ concern over high gas prices and participation in a foreign war don’t factor into his decisionmaking on Iran, The Atlantic reported he is thinking about how lower gas prices and demonstrated progress with Iran can impact the elections.

The Pentagon has instructed U.S. Central Command to conclude preparations for a renewed military campaign against Iran, Axios reported Wednesday, citing U.S. officials.

The president is weighing the timing of the strikes, according to the outlet, considering whether to launch them before the Nov. 3 elections — and possibly the Israeli elections, which take place on Oct. 27.

The bombing campaign is likely to include Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets, Axios reported, and may lead to increased gas prices in the U.S.

Between 9,000 and 10,000 more troops are expected to arrive in the Middle East by the end of November, The Wall Street Journal reported last week , dispatching a third aircraft carrier and an additional Marine expeditionary unit to the region.

There are already two carriers in the region, and if both remain, it will mark the first time since April that the U.S. has placed three carrier strike groups there, according to the Journal.

The U.S. and Iran struck a fragile ceasefire at that time, but it quickly fell apart and has devolved into sporadic fighting over the intervening months.

articles.title: More killed in Kramatorsk as Russia targets Ukraine’s transportation system
articles.summary: Russia’s attacks on trains, buses and ports are paralysing Ukraine’s transport network and endangering civilians.
articles.body:
Kyiv, Ukraine – A Russian glide bomb struck two passenger buses in the eastern Ukrainian town of Kramatorsk on Thursday morning, killing at least 30 people and wounding 18, regional authorities said.

Ukrainian officials said the attack was deliberate. When dropped from planes on the Russian side of the front line, such bombs can glide to fixed coordinates on the ground, in this case, a street in the town that lies about 20 kilometres (12.4 miles) from the front line.

“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” regional administration head Vadym Filashkin wrote on Telegram. “For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill the maximum number of people.”

“Russia consciously disregards all conceivable rules of warfare and norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians,” he wrote.

Filashkin ordered the suspension of the movement of all public transportation in Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk as Russia intensifies attacks, paralysing Ukraine’s transport infrastructure, from trains and minibuses to gas stations, bridges, seaports and freight ships.

“This is a new Russian tactic,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “They used to focus on depriving Ukraine of power, on switching off electricity and heating; now their task is also to immobilise the infrastructure, create a transportation collapse.”

“Unfortunately, Russia’s tactic has a certain effect with their strikes on railroads, gas stations,” he said. “They coerce to peace on their conditions.

“They also strike the public psychologically, disrupt the usual lifestyle in general.”

Throughout the war, Russia has denied it targets Ukrainian civilians, a statement that means little to Ukrainians. During the first eight months of 2026, 15,280 civilians were killed or injured, according to the United Nations – a toll that is 55 percent higher than during the same period in 2025.

With no civilian planes in the sky since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, trains, buses and trucks have become a lifeline for Ukrainian civilians and businesses, as well as for transporting military and humanitarian supplies.

Trains handle almost two-thirds of Ukraine’s freight volumes, including the export of steel slabs, grains and vegetable oils that keep the economy afloat.

At least 521 locomotives have been hit by drones and shelling since 2022, three-fifths this year alone, Ukrzaliznytsia, the state-run railway monopoly, said in late September.

Some locomotives were struck while in motion, and drones have occasionally hit passenger carriages, causing fires, deaths and injuries.

The largest such attack killed five passengers in January in the northeastern Kharkiv region, an act of “terrorism” that was “not militarily justified”, said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Hitting moving trains and buses has become possible because a new generation of Russian drones are no longer the slow, unmanned aircraft that can be jammed electronically or shot down with a machinegun or even an assault rifle.

Jet-powered, with bigger payloads, they are piloted by human operators who use a wireless mesh network, in which each drone serves as a relay node.

“They’re operated manually. The Russians improved their comms,” Andriy Pronin, one of the pioneers of drone warfare in Ukraine, told Al Jazeera.

Occasionally, the signal reaches the drones through a modem on the ground, on a rooftop or even inside somebody’s apartment – switched on by Ukrainians recruited by Russian intelligence, he said.

Locating the modems before attacks is “complicated, but doable”, Pronin said.

According to Ukrainian intelligence, prosecutors and officials, hundreds of recruits, including teenagers, have been offered money via Telegram. They often did not realise the consequences of their actions and have been arrested and convicted.

The video feed and geolocation are often backed by smuggled Ukrainian SIM cards or signals from mobile phone providers in neighbouring, pro-Moscow Belarus, officials believe. These drones can now get almost anywhere in Ukraine, including once-safe western regions.

A train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson crossed into Poland on September 14, just 30 minutes before a Russian drone struck another passenger train’s locomotive at Yahodyn train station in western Ukraine. Former CIA chief David Petraeus was on a nearby train and reportedly described the attack as “terrifying” and “the act of a truly barbaric leader”.

Ukrainian civilians are equally terrified.

When a daytime Russian drone attack began on September 23, Alyna realised that her workplace was in the most vulnerable place in Kyiv’s central railway station.

She works in a cafeteria located almost in the middle of a massive overpass that stretches above 14 main tracks between the station’s main buildings.

The howling air raid siren and the booms of exploding jet-powered kamikaze drones sent the 24-year-old Kyiv resident scurrying down the stairs and farther on to the subway station.

The drones hit a nearby market, sending black plumes of smoke into the sky and burning to the ground the rotund, modernist building known as the Puck.

“Everything was whistling and rattling above me,” Alyna told Al Jazeera just after another air raid alert ended and passengers began re-entering the station. She withheld her last name for security purposes.

Minutes after the conversation, one more air raid siren forced the passengers out of the railway station, and a drone hit by an interceptor turned into a black cloud in the sky a couple of kilometres east of the building.

The attacks are not limited to trains – Russian drones target petrol stations, buses and minibuses, and seaports, paralysing Ukraine’s exports of grain, vegetable oils and steel.

“You go to a minibus and can hear how [drones] buzz right next to it,” Tetiana Melikhova, a university professor in Zaporizhzhia, a southeastern city with a pre-war population of 720,000, told Al Jazeera.

Her 18-year-old student, Tetiana Bubynets , and two other civilians aged 31 and 48 were killed by an AI-driven drone that was programmed to strike a petrol station on July 6.

articles.title: Guilfoyle asked GOP donor to wire her $100K for AmEx bill: Wall Street Journal report
articles.summary: Days before her confirmation hearing last year, U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle asked one of President Trump’s donors to wire her American Express account $100,000, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday. “You could just send it here. It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” she wrote to Eric Deters…
articles.body:
Days before her confirmation hearing last year, U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle asked one of President Trump’s donors to wire her American Express account $100,000, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday.

“You could just send it here. It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” she wrote to Eric Deters on Signal, the Journal reported . “Please.”

Guilfoyle also sent Deters instructions on how to wire money to her American Express account and called the Trump donor twice, according to the outlet. The then-nominee to lead the U.S. Embassy asked Deters to wire her the money on July 3, 2025, six days before her confirmation hearing before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

The panel greenlighted her nomination in a 13-9 vote, and the full Senate confirmed her nomination via a 51-47 tally in September of last year.

Guilfoyle, the ex-wife of California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), was engaged to Donald Trump Jr. until the two broke up in 2024. The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment on the Journal’s report.

Deters, who has run for governor of Kentucky and for Congress, is the former co-owner of Snappy Tomato Pizza. The Kentucky Bar Association has suspended him twice, the Journal reported.

In 2022, Deters donated $125,000 to the MAGA Inc. super PAC, according to data from the Federal Election Commission.

When Guilfoyle asked Deters to wire her the money, he shot her down, saying it would cost him his marriage.

“Your needing $100,000 urgent unfortunately is not going to work,” Deters reportedly wrote to Guilfoyle. “I can’t do this without getting a divorce.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to comment on the story, telling reporters in Greece he does not “even know if it’s true or not.”

Rubio said, “I’m not going to comment on a story that literally posted a few hours ago.”

The Journal also recently reported on Guilfoyle allegedly promoting a Greek company whose lobbyist traveled alongside her for meetings with foreign governments in the Balkans.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.), the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations panel, sent Rubio a letter last week asking him to review the report’s details .

“Such actions do not serve U.S. credibility overseas and risk undermining U.S. diplomacy,” Shaheen wrote to her former Senate colleague, referencing the report.

images.caption: Kimberly Guilfoyle, nominee to be an ambassador to Greece, arrives for her Senate Foreign Relations Committee nomination hearing on July 9, 2025.

articles.title: Rubio refuses to comment on Guilfoyle allegations
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio batted away questions Thursday about the conduct of President Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle. The Wall Street Journal reported this week that Guilfoyle solicited cash in exchange for influence with the Trump administration, as part of an effort to pay her debts during the confirmation process for her current…
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio batted away questions Thursday about the conduct of President Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle.

The Wall Street Journal reported this week that Guilfoyle solicited cash in exchange for influence with the Trump administration, as part of an effort to pay her debts during the confirmation process for her current role.

The Journal reported last month that the former Fox News host and ex-fiancee of the president’s son gave preferential treatment to a Greek shipping firm , causing Democrats to raise alarm that she’s undermining U.S. policy in the region.

Rubio, responding to reporters’ questions Thursday morning while on diplomatic travel in Greece, said he was not going to comment on the latest story, published Wednesday evening.

“Like, our job is not to respond every time someone decides to give the media something without any advance warning, without having any chance to look at it and see what’s in there,” he said.

“That’s not the way — that’s not the way you run an organization, and that’s not a serious way to conduct the policy of our country.”

Rubio said he didn’t know if the stories against Guilfoyle are “true or not true.”

“So it’s just not going to work that way, and it most certainly is not going to work that way when I’m sitting in another country. All right?”

The Wednesday report from the Journal detailed how Guilfoyle solicited $100,000 for her credit card bill from a Trump donor in a way that wouldn’t leave a paper trail.

“What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing,” she wrote at one point to the donor, a businessman and former lawyer named Eric Deters.

It was the second time on his trip that Rubio was faced with tough questions about Guilfoyle’s conduct.

Rubio, standing next to Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis on Wednesday, was asked if her involvement in energy dealings complied with State Department ethics.

In September, the Journal reported the ambassador gave preferential access to a Greek energy company in multinational discussions over energy infrastructure. The report also detailed an exchange in which Guilfoyle threatened that the U.S. could bring down a foreign democratic government.

“This is not the forum where we’re going to address that, as simple as that. Suffice it to say our embassy here is doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here,” Rubio said Wednesday.

“The questions you’re asking me, we’re not addressing those at press conferences in Greece with the foreign minister and in another country.”

The top Democrats on the House and Senate foreign affairs panels wrote to Rubio in separate letters last week raising deep concern over the reports about Guilfoyle’s conduct.

“If these reports are accurate, Ambassador Guilfoyle is unfit to represent the United States abroad and should be removed from her position,” Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, wrote on Sept. 30 .

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the outgoing ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations panel, called for “an immediate review of Ambassador Guilfoyle’s actions, and a clarification of what steps have and will be taken to avoid undue influence and even the appearance of a conflict of interest.”

images.caption: Kim Guilfoyle addresses the Republican National Convention at Fiserv Forum in Milwaukee, July 17, 2024.

articles.title: ‘I don’t care if I go to jail’: Newly released video shows 6-year-old defiant after Virginia school shooting
articles.summary: A 6-year-old boy who shot his Virginia elementary school teacher in 2023 is seen cursing at police officers in a newly released body camera video.
articles.body: A 6-year-old boy who shot his Virginia elementary school teacher in 2023 is seen cursing at police officers in a newly released body camera video. “Where is the weapon?” one officer asks. “It’s over there,” the child says, cursing at the officer. “If you want a piece of me, come it all, b----,” the child says. The video shows the moments after the first-grader shot Abigail Zwerner at Richneck Elementary School in Newport News on Jan. 6, 2023. The bullet tore through her hand before striking her in the chest, where it remains. At a civil trial against the school’s former assistant principal, Ebony Parker, a doctor testified that removing the bullet would be far more dangerous than leaving it in place. Zwerner testified at the trial that she thought she was dying after she was shot. “I thought I was on my way to heaven or in heaven,” she said. “But then it all got black.” Zwerner, who no longer teaches, was awarded $10 million in damages, plus interest, last year, after a jury found that Parker ignored warnings that the child had a gun in his backpack. The jury said that the shooting could have been avoided and that Parker’s gross negligence led to the incident. In the video, the child also appears to curse at a different teacher, who is restraining him as police begin processing the scene. “My mom had that,” the child says, in reference to the gun. “I stole that from my mom.” At another point, the child screams at the officers. “Both of y’all want a f---ing piece of me, b----,” he says. The teacher holding him says the child still has gun residue on his hands. The video was initially sealed during Parker’s criminal trial, where she was charged with eight counts of child neglect. A judge dismissed the case in May, ruling that Parker had not committed a crime under state law. The judge decided to release the video but ordered the child’s face be blurred. “I don’t care if you call backup,” the child tells police. “I don’t care if I go to jail.” The child’s mother, Deja Taylor, was arrested after the shooting on a state charge of felony child neglect and a federal weapons charge. In 2023 she was sentenced to two years in prison on the child neglect charge and 21 months on the weapons charge.

articles.title: TikToker Kalani Ghost Hunter praises South West takeaways
articles.summary: Food venues report a surge in sales following visit from Kalani Ghost Hunter.
articles.body:
A TikToker from Tennessee who became "obsessed" with British food has given his seal of approval to takeaway nosh in Devon and Cornwall.

Kalani Smith, who goes by Kalani Ghost Hunter online, racks up millions of views posting his reviews on social media and he recently finished a tour of the South West.

He sampled pasties, spicy spuds and a local ale on his visit - and he explained he learned the hard way about the jam and cream rivalry that remains a heavily contested point between the counties.

Georgie Morgia, who runs Mrs Browns Bakery in Plymouth, said "everyone was a bit blown away" when Smith walked in and she reported a surge in sales after the business was reviewed.

Smith said he had a "wonderful time" in the South West, adding: "The folks down there are really nice.

"But something I picked up on very quickly is you don't want to get in between the Devon-Cornwall debate because there's no winning."

Smith said he found himself in a difficult position when explaining why he applies cream first on a scone in Cornwall, which typically favours jam first.

"I just look at the cream as butter," he said.

"I put the cream on first then the jam, but the moment I brought that up in Cornwall, it was not a good sight."

Morgia, who runs three Mrs Browns Bakery shops in Plymouth, said staff were "making the most" of the surge in sales after the visit.

"Everyone was a bit blown away because we are fans of him and we watch his videos," she said.

"The pressures and financial pressures are crazy, but for Kalani coming in, honestly it has just changed everything at the minute.

"All three shops have sold-out, we've been waking up at 3am and selling out.

"We know it won't last forever so we are just making the most of it, the people of Plymouth coming in and finding out about us, it's just fantastic and we are super grateful for it."

Smith said he "loved to hear" the news of the surge in sales, adding: "Some people don't realise that I'm not looking to get paid by anybody, like everything that I do is just because I find it and want to go experience it.

"If I post about it, I just want to share it - so it's always nice to help out a local business and that makes me happy that folks went down there and tried them out."

Another spot visited by Smith was The Nobody Inn pub in the Devon village of Doddiscombsleigh, which he described as "cosy".

He tried a prawn cocktail, steak pie and a local ale during the visit.

Chris Canevali, who manages the pub alongside his partner Coral, said the visit was unplanned and a "great surprise".

"He just appeared on Monday evening and started recording his video, it has been fantastic since," he said.

"We had no idea who he was until he had been and gone and uploaded his video after - it was a great surprise really.

"We have immediately had more people booking in, it's been great."

The TikToker then made his way to West Park Chippy in Plymouth, where he sampled the local delicacy of spicy spuds.

After sampling the potatoes covered in batter, Smith said: "I honestly don't know why these aren't at every chippy in the UK."

articles.title: Zambia signs US health aid deal after disputes over data-sharing
articles.summary: The US will provide $1.5bn (£1.1bn) under the deal that was negotiated after Trump cut USAID funding.
articles.body:
Zambia has signed a five-year health financing agreement with the US, ending months of public dispute over whether the country was trading citizens' medical data and mineral rights for aid.

Under the memorandum of understanding, signed in Lusaka on Thursday along with a data-sharing deal, the US will provide about $1.5bn (£1.1bn), with Zambia also contributing.

Civil society groups had criticised a leaked draft they said allowed too much data sharing, while activists seized on reports that health money was being linked to preferential access for US companies to minerals, which the then-US ambassador denied.

US President Donald Trump had accused USAID of wasteful spending. After closing the agency last year, Washington has pursued similar deals with a number of African countries, arguing partner governments should take on more of the cost.

Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda are among those that have signed. Ghana and Zimbabwe have rejected agreements over conditions about sharing data and specimens.

Officials say the revised text of Zambia's new deal addresses concerns about privacy, intellectual property and benefit-sharing.

Health Minister Roma Chilengi said earlier this week that clauses requiring Zambia to send biological specimens to the US had been removed, and that the agreement would not allow the sharing of individual patient records.

Data exchange, he said, would be limited to information needed to monitor and evaluate programmes funded under the deal.

Why some African nations are turning down Trump aid money

A draft leaked earlier this year prompted civil society groups to warn that Zambia was accepting wider data-sharing terms than other African countries, including long-term access to pathogen information and specimens.

The Chapter One Foundation, a human rights group, said the government risked "signing away" citizens' health data. HIV advocates, including the Treatment Advocacy and Literacy Campaign, said the flow of information would be one-way and demanded the text be published.

Opposition figures and activists also seized on reports that health money was being linked to preferential access for US companies to Zambia's large reserves of copper and other critical minerals.

In May, Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe called the data terms a violation of privacy and "unconscionable", and accused Washington of tying the package to minerals. Then-US ambassador, Michael Gonzales, rejected that account as false.

The row was sharpened by an earlier US suspension of drug funding after the embassy alleged theft of donated medicines, which the government disputed.

Zambia's new deal replaces support that for years flowed largely through US programmes. The money is intended to support HIV/Aids, tuberculosis, malaria, maternal and child health, disease surveillance and wider health system work, including the recruitment of community health workers.

The US has described the arrangement as a shift from a donor-recipient model towards shared responsibility, with US funding expected to decline over the five years as Zambia increases domestic spending.

Officials have put the combined package covering 2026 to 2030 at roughly $3.6bn, though figures for the Zambian share have varied.

Shortly after taking office for the second time in January 2025, Trump ordered the closure of USAID, in the process decimating health programmes in some African countries that relied on American funding.

Critics say the move has impacted the speed of detecting the current ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and the scale of the response, emphasising that the humanitarian agency was crucial to organising logistics, supplies and local outreach.

The US denies its cuts have harmed efforts, arguing that they are more "aligned and effective" under the new arrangement and pointing to the $270m it has donated to tackle the epidemic.
