articles.title: Why the National Hurricane Center bet big on AI to forecast Isaias
articles.summary: In forecasting Hurricane Isaias, meteorologists at the National Hurricane Center in Miami have shaped their predictions to closely match an AI hurricane model.
articles.body: From the time Hurricane Isaias first formed, meteorologists at the National Hurricane Center made a big bet. They shaped their predictions to closely match an AI hurricane model developed by Google DeepMind, rather than leaning on the classic physics-based models many Americans are more familiar with, such as the European and GFS. So far, the bet has paid off. Forecasts for this storm reflect the improving reliability of AI weather models overall, and signal an astonishingly rapid shift to routine use of such products by human forecasters. Relying heavily on DeepMind meant NHC forecast Isaias would become a Category 2 from the first advisory on Tuesday, when it didn’t even have a name yet. At that point, many of the physics-based computer models, which rely on mathematical equations describing how the atmosphere works to simulate future weather conditions, were vacillating between different projections but generally forecasting a weaker storm that would take a different track than the DeepMind and other AI models were showing. If the forecast is accurate, it will mark a huge victory for Google and help the people in the path of the storm, who will have had more time to prepare for a significantly stronger blow. Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the tropical Atlantic season, due largely to the effects of a super El Niño in the Pacific, setting a record for the ocean basin’s latest first hurricane of the season. The confidence of NHC forecasters in Google DeepMind model in particular — the newest iteration of which is WeatherNext 3 — stems largely from experience. Last season the Hurricane Center correctly anticipated the rapid intensification of Hurricane Melissa almost three days before its devastating arrival in Jamaica based largely on the projections from DeepMind. It also stems from the fact that the Hurricane Center partnered with Google to help train the model and learn more about its capabilities. As is occurring in many fields right now, the world of meteorology is undergoing rapid advancements due to AI, although these models are used in conjunction with the traditional physics models, which still have their advantages. AI models are trained on past weather events and, in the case of DeepMind’s, are also given current weather data. DeepMind performed extremely well last season, according to NHC director Michael Brennan, and has been accurate in anticipating the intensity of many Pacific Ocean storms this season. “The AI models have shown more consistency” from one model run to the next, Brennan said regarding the reliance on DeepMind for Hurricane Isaias. “It’s a combination of probably what we were seeing from looking at these physics-based models and some of the inconsistency there, and then just the performance of the AI guidance so far, and the fact that it has proven to be pretty reliable,” Brennan said. Part of that proof came from a gutsy call that the Hurricane Center forecasters made last year during Hurricane Melissa. Last season, in a first, Hurricane Center forecasters explicitly forecast that Hurricane Melissa would reach Category 5 intensity when it was just an 80-mph Category 1 hurricane, largely by relying on the clear projections from DeepMind. In fact, by some measures, DeepMind even outperformed human forecasters during the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season overall. With global climate change enabling more tropical cyclones to rapidly intensify, the Hurricane Center has been making more bullish first forecasts for certain storms, including Isaias. Before AI stepped onto the forecasting stage, the NHC had employed more of a stair-step approach, gradually raising the intensity ceiling of a storm as it revved up, which often put the official forecasts behind the curve. That practice seems to have ended. Rapidly intensifying storms are now more common, and the latest models are better able to anticipate it. “We’ve definitely been making more aggressive intensity forecasts overall for the last several years, and we certainly do have more confidence to try to make some of these more aggressive intensity forecasts early on, like we did for Melissa last year, but we’ve also done for Helene and Milton,” Brennan said. He cited physical computer model support for rapid intensification plus weather forecasters’ understanding of the environment in which a storm is forming as additional factors allowing early predictions of rapid intensification. “It’s not just one thing, but certainly the AI models have done pretty well in some of those cases,” Brennan said. “So it’s another tool in the toolbox, so to speak, or another piece of evidence that can help support those more aggressive intensity forecasts,” he said of the AI models. Brennan said forecasters are not skittish about relying on DeepMind in part because they know the training data that went into it. “I think the most important thing is to make sure that the models are trained on the most accurate data we have,” he said, “and we’ve worked with Google to help them train on our best track analysis, and that’s one reason why I think their performance has improved in terms of intensity forecasting relative to some of the earlier AI models that did well for track, but did not do well for intensity.” Those models had been trained on large-scale data sets that weren’t hurricane-specific, he said. Meanwhile, Hurricane Isaias is churning its way toward the northeastern Gulf Coast and is likely to make landfall as a hurricane, according to a consensus of most computer models — not just DeepMind.

articles.title: In 2024, Washington opened a first-in-the-nation eight-story spiral passage through a dam; young sockeye salmon could finally reach the river downstream
articles.summary: Washington has unveiled an innovative eight-story spiral fish passage at Cle Elum Dam, enabling young sockeye salmon to safely reach their downstream habitat for the first time in over 90 years. This groundbreaking facility could increase salmon populations significantly and restore vital river ecosystems.
articles.body: Washington completed a juvenile fish passage facility at Cle Elum Dam in 2024 with an eight-story-deep concrete helix that was designed to carry young salmon from the reservoir around the dam and into the Cle Elum River downstream. The state Department of Ecology described the structure as the first of its kind in the nation.The facility is part of the Yakima Basin Integrated Plan, with the intention of restoring fish passage at a dam that had separated salmon from habitat farther upstream, and the larger project is expected to provide access to about 30 miles of river habitat. Washington officials project that improved passage could help increase sockeye returns to the Yakima Basin from about 20,000 to 100,000 fish a year.The dam needed a way aroundCle Elum Dam was built in 1933 and stores water in the Cle Elum Reservoir. It created a barrier for fish that were moving between the reservoir and the river below it, and the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation began developing a downstream passage design specifically for Cle Elum. Its hydraulic research examined how juvenile sockeye salmon could safely travel more than 80 feet downward through a compact structure while still being able to maintain stable flow conditions.The resulting design combines a multilevel intake, the helix, a tunnel, and an outfall downstream of the dam; the intake allows fish to enter at different reservoir levels, while the helix carries them downward before they continue through the tunnel toward the river.The helix works like a giant waterslideThe concrete structure is similar to a spiral parking-ramp or waterslide, and fish enter from the reservoir and travel down the helix tail-first. Washington's Department of Ecology said that the fish can travel through the structure at speeds of up to 25 miles per hour, and the design was developed to reduce turbulence and provide a relatively smooth passage, with the trip through the helix itself taking about a minute. The helix drops the fish more than 80 feet in elevation before they enter a tunnel that leads to the Cle Elum River downstream of the dam.The concept had been tested long before construction began, with Bureau of Reclamation engineers using both numerical models and physical hydraulic models to refine the helix design and determine the geometry that was needed for continuous downstream fish passage. The modeling examined water flow through the structure and helped engineers develop a stable area within the channel where juvenile fish could travel safely.Young salmon began using the systemThe Bureau of Reclamation reported releasing thousands of young salmon through the newly built helix passage system in May 2024, which included hatchery-raised coho and wild-caught salmon, and researchers planned to track their survival as they moved downstream through the Yakima River toward the Pacific Ocean. The system initially benefits juvenile sockeye, while the wider fish-passage and reintroduction program also involves coho, spring Chinook, steelhead and Pacific lamprey. The Bureau of Reclamation says that the project is intended to restore access to habitat that was cut off when the dam was built.The Cle Elum facility therefore tackles a very specific problem that was created by a high dam, which is getting young fish out of a reservoir and into the river without sending them directly over the dam. Its eight-story helix provides that downstream route while engineers and fisheries agencies continue monitoring how fish use the system.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Trump says US will not strike Iran before midterms
articles.summary: President Trump said Thursday the U.S. military will not launch strikes against Iran before the midterm elections, claiming the administration is having “productive discussions” with the Islamic Republic. “I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in…
articles.body:
President Trump said Thursday the U.S. military will not launch strikes against Iran before the midterm elections, claiming the administration is having “productive discussions” with the Islamic Republic.

“I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait (22 Million Barrels, last night alone, with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran!), we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” the president wrote on Truth Social .

“IRAN WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON,” Trump added.

The post comes as the president has been weighing whether to resume major combat operations before the November elections.

The White House asked the Pentagon to develop strike options against Iranian targets that could be exercised before the midterms, The Atlantic reported on Wednesday.

The White House said Trump has “all options” available on what the next steps are on Iran.

“The Commander-in-Chief has all options available at any time,” a White House official told The Hill earlier Thursday. “The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing.”

“Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways; the easy way or the hard way. President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States,” the official said.

The U.S. and Iran’s diplomatic progress has stalled as the war reached well into its seventh month.

Tehran is facing economic strains as the Trump administration has continued its economic pressure campaign and naval blockade in the Arabian Sea. But the Iranian military has continued striking commercial tankers attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting energy exports.

The musing over potentially authorizing strikes against Iran comes as the Trump administration has surged more U.S. forces to the U.S. Central Command (Centcom) region.

The Pentagon dispatched more than 4,000 Marines and sailors aboard three warships, led by USS Makin Island, a Wasp-class amphibious assault ship, to Centcom theater.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt, a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, is sailing toward the Middle East to relieve the USS George Washington.

Oil prices also surged amid reports of Iran strikes before the November elections.

Brent crude went up to $104.60 per barrel on Thursday and West Texas Intermediate jumped 3.91 percent and was at $92.19 per barrel.

articles.title: Green Cards red-carded: MAGA benches India-linked IT firms from PERM process
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent from Washington: The Trump administration on Thursday suspended eight major Indian or strongly India-linked tech companies from the US
articles.body: TOI Correspondent from Washington: The Trump administration on Thursday suspended eight major Indian or strongly India-linked tech companies from the US program used by employers to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residence (green card), a move that could affect tens of thousands of Indian IT professionals.The administration also announced investigations into nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, over allegations that international students and foreign workers are being used to reduce labour costs or compromise federally funded research.In more strikes against global companies and foreigners, mainly Indians, accused of "stealing American jobs,” Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling, with veep JD Vance standing alongside, announced that the Department of Labour was suspending Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe from the Permanent Labour Certification, or PERM, program.PERM is an important step in the employment-based green-card process; before sponsoring most foreign workers for employment-based permanent residence, an employer must generally obtain certification from the Labour Department that there are not sufficient qualified, willing and available US workers for the particular position and that hiring the foreign worker will not adversely affect US wages and working conditions.According to Sonderling, the eight companies had collectively requested almost three million foreign workers since 2009, received more than 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and obtained more than 100,000 permanent labour certifications. "That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers," he asserted, declaring that the DOL would not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies.However, industry veterans say H-1B approvals and PERM certifications measure foreign workers hired or sponsored, not Americans who lost jobs. Studies by the Census Bureau and National Academies have found little evidence of broad displacement of native-born workers from skilled immigration. The figures show the scale of foreign-worker hiring by the companies, but not how many of those jobs would otherwise have gone to Americans. The tech industry insists the US simply does not produce enough STEM graduates to meet demand.For now, the suspension primarily affects the transition from temporary employment to permanent residence but does not for now cancel H-1B visas or immediately prevent the affected companies from employing foreign workers. But the impact of PERM suspension will be significant for Indian tech workers because Indian nationals account for a large share of H-1B workers and employment-based green-card applicants. Many Indian professionals work for large tech services companies such as Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL and Cognizant while waiting for their employers to sponsor them for permanent residence.While the suspension does not automatically invalidate PERM certifications that have already been approved nor prevent an employee from obtaining employment-based permanent residence through another employer that is not subject to the suspension, the consequences could be more serious for H-1B workers approaching the six-year limit on their temporary status. Under US immigration law, certain H-1B workers can obtain extensions beyond six years when they have reached particular stages of the employment-based green-card process. Delays in starting or advancing a PERM case can therefore become an immigration problem for workers who are close to that deadline.Unlike some of the Trump administration's other immigration initiatives, Thursday's action does not appear to require the government to first issue a new regulation and seek public comments. Existing DOL regulations give the agency authority to suspend processing of PERM applications when it has reason to believe that an employer, attorney or agent may have engaged in fraud or willful misrepresentation, or when an investigation is under way. The regulations permit a suspension for an initial period of up to 180 days and allow it to continue under certain circumstances. However, the affected companies could still challenge the action in federal court.The administration has presented the move as part of a broader effort to make American companies hire more US workers. "Our message to Microsoft is: You're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers," said Veep JD Vance, whose presence at the announcement also gave the action a broader political significance. Immigration and foreign-worker policy have become central issues for the administration's America First agenda, particularly on the eve of mid-term elections, and Vance has emerged as a strong advocate for reducing what he describes as excessive corporate dependence on foreign labour.Incidentally, of the eight companies that face PERM suspension, two US-based companies, Microsoft and Adobe, have Indian-American CEOs (Satya Nadella and Shantanu Narayen transitioning to Anil Chakravarthy), while Cap Gemini's CEO is Aiman Ezzat, an Egypt-born French national. Vance's position on the issue has attracted particular attention because he is married to Usha Vance, the US-born daughter of Indian immigrants who came to America through the academic route.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cornell Jane Doe faces death threats, doxxing after armed cops swarm family home
articles.summary: Cornell’s Jane Doe is terrified after armed police swarmed her parents’ home on Tuesday night following a fake call claiming a man had shot and killed his
articles.body: Cornell’s Jane Doe is terrified after armed police swarmed her parents’ home on Tuesday night following a fake call claiming a man had shot and killed his mother and sister. The incident came amid death threats, doxxing attempts and threatening calls against the woman, who has sued Cornell University and others alleging she was raped at a fraternity house in 2024.According to a report by CNN, her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said police pointed guns at Doe’s father, brother and boyfriend after responding to the bogus emergency call. The FBI is also looking into the incident.“She’s scared,” Giuffra said on Wednesday. “I don’t think she’s in a good spot now.”Police swarm home after fake shooting callPolice were called to Doe’s hometown at about 7pm Tuesday. The caller falsely claimed that a man had shot his mother and then his sister.An officer rushed to the family home believing there was an active shooter. He saw a car leaving the driveway and detained two men. They were later identified as Doe’s brother and boyfriend.Doe’s father then came out of the house.“I’m the dad. What’s going on?” he told police, according to the report.He also told officers that his daughter was the Jane Doe in the Cornell case. He said the family had been receiving threats.Giuffra said the incident could have turned deadly.“Luckily the brother was in his car, (he) put his hands up,” Giuffra said. “(Doe’s) boyfriend got thrown on the ground,” and her father also had “guns put in his face.”“If you had a trigger-happy cop, or somebody had done the wrong thing, somebody could have ended up dead,” he said.Threats escalate after lawsuitThe swatting attack came after weeks of threats against Doe.Giuffra said his client has received dozens of threats since she filed her 101-page lawsuit in September.The lawsuit names Cornell, the Chi Phi fraternity, seven fraternity members and others. It alleges that fraternity members drugged and sexually assaulted Doe in October 2024.It also alleges that members invited others to join the assault through a group chat. The seven students deny wrongdoing.Doe’s identity was redacted from the lawsuit. But online personalities have tried to uncover and publish her name.One person with a large following on X asked people to send him information identifying Doe. He later claimed he had identified her and said he posted the information before deleting it.Giuffra also said Doe received a text message on Monday containing three gun emojis.‘Otherwise blood will be shed’Doe received another threatening call shortly before police arrived at her home, according to her lawyer and police reports.She told officers she “began panicking” because her phone “wouldn’t stop ringing”.Giuffra’s wife also received a threatening call that night. It is unclear whether the calls were connected to the swatting attack.On Wednesday, Giuffra shared an audio recording with CNN of a call made to his office.A man identified himself as “the person who called your client”.“I’m telling you guys simply, I think you should advise your client to withdraw the case. Otherwise blood will be shed.”Giuffra said Doe was now so frightened that she was covering the windows of her parents’ home with paper.“She’s scared,” he said.Doe’s life ‘derailed’Doe had studied hotel administration at Cornell’s Nolan School of Hotel Administration. Her lawyer said attending Cornell had been her dream.She left the programme without graduating after the alleged assault.Earlier this year, she moved to New York City and tried to build a career in the hotel industry. She returned to her parents’ home after filing the lawsuit and facing intense public backlash.“The dream is lost,” Giuffra said.Doe now spends most of her time at home. She goes for walks and remains in contact with some Cornell friends.“She’s a little paranoid,” Giuffra said. “If she’s out of (the) safety zone of her family, she just doesn’t seem to function well.”Her mother has taken time off work to care for her.Cornell faces growing angerThe case has also triggered protests at Cornell.Students held a seven-hour sit-in on Wednesday in solidarity with Doe. The university is facing scrutiny over its handling of her allegations.Cornell has appointed former acting US attorney general Sally Yates to investigate its handling of sexual assault claims.University president Michael Kotlikoff acknowledged the anger on campus during a meeting with the Graduate and Professional Student Assembly on Monday.“We’re all angry. I understand that anger,” Kotlikoff said, according to the Cornell Daily Sun. “People want easy answers to this.”Cornell has previously said the case raises “heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization, and aspects of party culture, alcohol, and drug use.”Giuffra said Doe has also received messages of support from around the world.“The students up there (at Cornell) have been overwhelmingly supportive, and it’s wonderful,” he said. “They’re trying to effect change, and bringing out to the light something that’s been going on for generations.”You use AI every day. articles.title: 'I don't know what my partner earns': How soon into dating should you reveal your salary?
articles.summary: Talking about salary, spending habits and debt can be some of dating's trickier conversations.
articles.body:
You know their favourite restaurant, what happened with their ex and their most embarrassing childhood story. But do you know how much your partner earns?

Money remains one of dating's trickier conversations. Bring it up too early and it can sound like you're sizing up their bank balance. But leave it too long and you could be planning a future with someone without knowing much about their finances at all.

We spoke to 20-somethings in New York City to see if there was a sweet spot for when to talk salaries.

Willa Morton, 25, says she doesn't think couples necessarily need to reveal their salaries at all.

"It's just a number and you can gauge how much someone makes based on the way they live and how much they spend," she says.

Willa, who works in tech sales, has talked to her boyfriend about not earning very much herself but hasn't asked him for a figure in return.

He's a company founder and, though his income varies, she knows that he earns more than she does.

"He's more free-spending whereas I'm always saying, 'That's too expensive, that costs too much, we don't need to spend that.'"

Their dates typically cost around $200 (£150) and he usually pays, while she picks up smaller bills such as coffees.

"It's an unspoken rule that he will pick up the bigger bills."

For many, there's a fairly clear dividing line as to when you talk about salary, spending habits and debt and that's when you become an official couple.

Alexa Ludato, 25, who works in insurance, says she'd only have the conversation when she was official with someone.

Before then, she would "like to have an idea of what their job is, but not how much they make".

Her friend, Vik Sunderaj, 22, agrees. "You should only discuss it once you get into a serious relationship."

He thinks a salary question on the first few dates is "a little crazy".

"If they asked, I would be honest, but I wouldn't bring it up," he says. And if his date really wanted to know his salary, "it probably means they wouldn't be the right person for me".

Others feel even more strongly about being asked too soon. Twenty-six-year-old Bridget Shurdut, who works in sales, says she would find it "incredibly odd" if someone asked about her salary within the first few dates.

"I don't think I'd continue to see that person. I'd answer the question, but it would be a red flag for me."

For her, someone's current salary isn't necessarily particularly useful information anyway as she says she's much more interested in "whether someone is ambitious and driven than what they earn monetarily".

Dating and relationship coach Kate Mansfield, says money conversations "should start much earlier than many people think".

"In the first few dates you should talk about how each of you approaches spending, saving, generosity, lifestyle and financial independence as these things shape compatibility."

Becoming official doesn't necessarily mean swapping payslips though.

Insurance worker Emily Moretta, 26, has been with her boyfriend for two years and says they still haven't explicitly told each other their salaries and "he doesn't know how much I make".

She assumes he probably has a rough idea, but says neither has ever felt the need to ask.

"Maybe down the line we would, when it gets more serious," she says, adding that they would have to be at the stage of moving in together before talking about it.

articles.title: Two Latvian men arrested inside UK military base after breach
articles.summary: Police say nothing so far suggests the incident at RAF Molesworth linked to events surrounding RAF Fairford last month.
articles.body:
Two Latvian men have been arrested inside a military base in southeast England that houses United States and NATO intelligence hubs after the perimeter fence was breached, police have said.

The arrests come amid heightened concerns about security at military bases in the United Kingdom after a separate incident last month.

Counterterrorism police said on Thursday that the two men, aged 36 and 32, were arrested at the Royal Air Force (RAF) Molesworth base in Cambridgeshire.

They are being held on suspicion of trespass and of entering a prohibited place “for a purpose prejudicial to the UK”, said police.

A security patrol had spotted an abandoned vehicle near the base late on Wednesday night. Police found a “small breach” in the perimeter fence before locating and arresting the men in the early hours of Thursday, they said.

The men were taken to a police station in Cambridgeshire where they are still in custody. Both are Latvian nationals residing in the UK.

The arrests come after a major incident at RAF Fairford in western England on September 27 that led to the arrest of seven men, all in their 20s, who have since been released on bail. One is a dual UK-Iranian national.

Due to the nature of the incident, UK counterterrorism police are leading the investigation into the security breach, police said.

“We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites,” said Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London.

“But at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford,” she added.

Flanagan said that the investigation at RAF Molesworth is at an early stage but added that enquiries would home in on “any potential motivation as to why the men were present at the site”.

RAF Molesworth, formerly a World War II airbase, is now a non-flying facility managed by the United States Air Force.

US intelligence has based its operation centres for Europe and Africa at the base near Huntingdon. It is also a NATO intelligence hub, according to a Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) website.

On Sunday, US military planes were abruptly flown out of the RAF base at Fairford in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vehicles were seen near the base, prompting a major incident to be declared.

That base had been used by the US military to conduct strikes in its war against Iran.

articles.title: Massachusetts mom found dead, police searching for her son as person of interest
articles.summary: A woman was found dead in her home in Reading, Massachusetts, on Thursday morning, and investigators are searching for her son as a person of interest in the case.
articles.body: A woman was found dead in her home in Reading, Massachusetts, on Thursday morning, and investigators are searching for her son as a person of interest in the case. Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan said police were first called to the home on Center Avenue around 12:38 a.m. The caller reported that he’d found his wife dead inside the kitchen of the home. The couple’s 13-year-old son was home and unharmed. The couple’s older son, who lives in the home, was missing. The victim was identified as Andria Hanafin, 49. The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner is conducting an autopsy, but the cause of death is believed to be a gunshot wound. Police are searching for the older son, 22-year-old Ryan Hanafin, and his vehicle, a black 2010 Dodge Charger with Massachusetts license plate 2PSY15. He is unaccounted for and considered a person of interest, the DA said. Reading police added that Ryan Hanafin has a license to carry a gun, which was suspended Thursday morning. Police said he should be considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached. Anyone with information on his whereabouts is urged to call 911. Ryan Hanafin’s car was last seen driving on I-93 toward Tewksbury, around 7:25 p.m. on Wednesday. The DA said they believe this is a case of domestic violence, though the exact circumstances are under investigation. “This is first and foremost a terrible tragedy,” Ryan said. Police have no significant history at the house or with the family, the DA said. The husband reported that he left for work around 11 a.m. that day and returned around 11 p.m. The younger son last saw his mother alive around 5 p.m., when he left the home with friends. When he returned home around 9 a.m., he said he went straight to his room and did not see his mother. Aerial video showed a heavy police presence outside a residence, with yellow crime scene tape cordoning off the area. No further details have been released.

articles.title: Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis
articles.summary: Hundreds have pitched their tents in central Madrid, while the Spanish prime minister has called a snap election.
articles.body:
Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square.

Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis , she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause.

"It's the same problem as always," she says. "A lack of homes."

She adds: "Landlords are taking advantage of the situation to raise rentals, and then there's also Airbnb."

Jorge Moreno, a 19-year-old film-dubbing student who has also been living in a tent here in central Madrid for the last few days, agrees.

"There are so many homes standing empty because they have been bought by vulture funds and investment funds which hike up the rent of people living in properties until they get rid of them," says Jorge, who lives with his mother and fears it will be a long time before he can afford a home of his own.

"They've been making a business of housing for a long time," he adds. "But it's an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home."

His and Pierina's diagnoses are frequently voiced by fellow protesters, ordinary Spaniards and even the Spanish government.

On presenting a recent package of emergency measures to tackle the housing problem, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was legislating "against those who consider housing just another object on the market with which to speculate".

Those reforms were rejected by Congress, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election next month.

Nicuray and Moreno can point to the single case that sparked the current Spanish housing protest movement as proof that profit-driven practices are at the heart of the crisis: the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home after the investment firm that had bought it tried to persuade her to leave, then sharply increased her rent, which she was unable to pay.

Although the social backlash that followed caused the company to invite Abascal to return to her old home, she never did, dying in hospital on Wednesday .

Many others have their own stories of struggling with a soaring rental market.

Carmen Pérez is a retired widow, originally from Ecuador, who has been living in Spain for 17 years.

When she arrived, housing was relatively cheap and accessible, but - as costs have risen - she has been forced to move in with her daughter and son-in-law as she looks for somewhere affordable to rent.

"When a property is listed to rent, there's always a long waiting list," she says. "And the rent is always too high for me. All of this has affected my health - I've got depression, I don't have any stability or security."

Spain has seen an average rise in rental costs of 84% over the last 10 years, according to property outlet Idealista.

In the centre of the southern city of Málaga, the increase has been 113 %, and, in Marbella - just under 150%.

Such numbers have made housing Spaniards' biggest concern.

A recent study by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) showed how the broader Spanish population, like the protesters, want to see action taken against those perceived to be powerful movers in the housing market.

Some 72% wanted higher taxes introduced for those with 10 or more properties; 76% wanted limits on short-term tourist accommodation; and 40% supported the expropriation of empty homes.

However, Jorge Galindo, director at the Esade centre for economic policy, says that available data makes it difficult to know exactly how many Spanish properties are owned by so-called "vulture funds" and being used for speculation.

He points to Bank of Spain figures from 2024 showing that only 8% of properties for rent are owned by companies.

Galindo says he concludes from the data available that there is not a notable accumulation of property to rent among a small number of owners in Spain.

"When it comes to explaining the rise in rentals, that is not the big cause," he says. "What explains it is the shortage of supply compared to demand over recent years."

The Bank of Spain appears to agree, and has estimated that the country has a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes.

The institution's deputy governor, Soledad Núñez, warned in September that by 2028 that could rise to one million.

There are 3.8 million empty properties in Spain, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), but a large number of those are in depopulated rural areas and therefore have little relevance to the current crisis, which is most acute in urban hubs.

Other explanations for this high number include properties awaiting renovation, or legal disputes between family members who have inherited them.

Demographic changes play a major part in the imbalance between supply and demand.

Between 2021 and 2025, there were about 1.2 million new households in Spain, driven in great part by the arrival of migrants who have played a major role in the country's recent economic growth.

However, house building has not kept pace, with fewer than half-a-million new homes during that period.

That was partly because Spain's construction industry had shrunk in the wake of the Eurozone crisis, while the cost of materials rose substantially after Covid, and a lack of political consensus put legal obstacles in the way of building.

"It was not a priority for us to build new houses," Galindo says. "But, once the demographic boom came, we realised how costly it was for us."

He adds that short-term tourist accommodation, like Airbnb, which has been identified by both the Spanish government and many activists as a culprit, is likely to have had a more localised effect, pushing up prices in specific urban areas rather than having an overall impact.

Meanwhile, the crisis has been aggravated by lagging salaries.

A study by El País found that, in real terms, the average Spaniard had 5% less spending power than a decade ago, due to taxes, social security and inflation. The average monthly salary in the Madrid region is €1,550 (£1,314; $1,738).

"No worker should have to spend 75% or 80% of their salary on rent, because what are they supposed to eat?" says Francisco Pardo, an 81-year-old retired taxi driver, who sympathises with the protesters, during a visit to the tent city in Madrid.

"Many workers don't even earn €2,000 [per month]."

The case of Maricarmen has suddenly made the housing crisis an urgent topic of discussion, not just in Madrid's Puerta del Sol but across the country.

The question now is whether a consensus can be reached on how to solve it.

articles.title: Golden statue depicting Trump nude appears at European Parliament
articles.summary: A golden statue of a nude President Trump appeared inside the European Parliament as part of a two-day exhibition this week. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico on Thursday called for its removal, although it had already been taken down. Danish artist Jens Galschiøt installed his sculpture, called “The Orange Plague,” in the building in Strasbourg,…
articles.body:
A golden statue of a nude President Trump appeared inside the European Parliament as part of a two-day exhibition this week.

Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico on Thursday called for its removal, although it had already been taken down.

Danish artist Jens Galschiøt installed his sculpture, called “The Orange Plague,” in the building in Strasbourg, France, on Tuesday. Trump is depicted as nude and covered in 23-karat gold leaf, with his legs around the shoulders of a bronze-colored, frail man atop a short pedestal.

Below the statue reads the text: “I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back.”

Fico called the statue “a sign of the decline of the European Union” and urged European Parliament President Roberta Metsola to remove it.

“The mocking statue of U.S. President Donald Trump displayed on the premises of the European Parliament is a sign of the decline of the entire EU,” he wrote on the social platform X . “I do not agree with all of the American president’s policies, not by a long shot. But at a time that calls for dialogue and mutual respect, insulting our partners on official premises demonstrates a profound failure to understand the times we live in.”

The prime minister called it “sad” that the EU “can no longer distinguish between the legitimate right to hold a different opinion and the actions of spiritually bankrupt individuals, adventurers and lunatics.”

Galschiøt promoted the statue on his X account, writing on Wednesday that he was handing out 10,000 miniature versions of the statue to the parliamentary building’s visitors. A post on Monday showed the statue covered in orange cloth before it was unveiled.

“Tomorrow I reveal the sculpture in the European Parliament. I hope it is well received and that it sparks a debate about friendship and power dynamics,” he wrote .

Galschiøt, known for politically provocative art , wrote on his website that the work was inspired by Hans Christian Anderson’s “The Emperor Wears No Clothes.” He called the statue “a satirical outcry against Trump and the U.S. assault on the green transition and the rule-based world order.”

“Trump is depicted as a self-proclaimed King of Justice,” he continued. “He sits on the back of a frail man, holding a golf club next to a world-shaped golf ball in one hand, and scales symbolizing his power to define justice in the other hand.”

The legislative body’s press service told The Hill that the statue was removed later on Wednesday.

The sculpture was installed as part of a two-day exhibition led by Danish left-wing Member of the European Parliament (MEP) Per Clausen. The European Parliament stated that MEPs must have any installations approved in advance by quaestors, who are tasked with overseeing administrative and financial matters.

“The rules in place outline that cultural events and exhibitions shall under no circumstances be offensive or of an inflammatory nature or contradictory to the values on which the Union is founded or likely to give rise to disturbances in the designated exhibition areas,” the press office told The Hill.

Clausen said in a statement that no one should “accept living in fear and self-censorship” and that anyone “so thin-skinned that you cannot handle this sculpture being exhibited in the European Parliament, then you do not belong on the world stage.”

articles.title: Yogi govt spent over Rs 17K crore on prison modernisation in 9.5 years
articles.summary: Yogi Adityanath govt spent Rs 17,000+ crore in 9.5 years to modernise UP prisons, boost security, and expand capacity with new jails planned.
articles.body: Lucknow: Yogi Adityanath govt has spent over Rs 17,000 crore over the past nine-and-a-half years to modernise Uttar Pradesh’s prison system, strengthen security and upgrade infrastructure, a senior official said on Thursday.Director General, Prisons and Correctional Services, PC Meena said state govt has focused not only on strengthening law and order but also on making prisons more responsive to contemporary requirements.“Efforts have been made to expand prison capacity and improve security and administrative arrangements through modern infrastructure and technology,” Meena said.He said the prison department’s budget has witnessed a sharp increase during the period. The allocation rose from Rs 913.07 crore in 2017-18 to Rs 2,877.58 crore in 2026-27, an increase of about 215%.According to officials, the department received a cumulative budget of Rs 5,494.41 crore between 2017-18 and 2021-22. The allocation increased to Rs 11,913.53 crore during the 2022-23 to 2026-27 period.“This increase reflects govt’s commitment to the development and modernisation of prisons,” Meena said.The state is also expanding inmate capacity and constructing new district prisons. Jails are being built in Amethi at a cost of Rs 176.12 crore, Mahoba (Rs 203.42 crore), Hathras (Rs 184.94 crore), Kushinagar (Rs 228.31 crore), Jaunpur (Rs 179.79 crore) and Hapur (Rs 190.08 crore).In addition, the process of acquiring land for proposed prisons is underway. articles.title: Survey finds chromium contamination up to 59 times limit near Chakeri Airport
articles.summary: Soil near Kanpur’s former Chakeri Airport terminal shows chromium up to 59x the limit, says IIT-Kanpur survey report submitted to the NGT.
articles.body: Kanpur: Soil samples near the former Chakeri Airport terminal in Kanpur were found to contain chromium levels up to 59 times the regulatory threshold, according to a survey report submitted by the Indian Institute of Technology-Kanpur (IIT-Kanpur) to the National Green Tribunal (NGT) on Oct 5.At the request of the district administration, IIT-Kanpur investigated chromium and mercury contamination in Kanpur Nagar, Kanpur Dehat and Fatehpur. UP govt standing counsel Bhanwar Pal Singh Jadaun presented the report before the NGT.Survey work was completed in the Jajmau industrial area, one of eight critical pollution zones in Kanpur Nagar, while a preliminary assessment began in Ruma. IIT-Kanpur collected 121 samples on July 16, Aug 10 and Aug 13.The July 16 sampling comprised 11 soil samples, 10 surface-water samples and 12 groundwater samples. On Aug 10, researchers collected 21 soil, 11 surface-water and 17 groundwater samples. On Aug 13, they collected 17 soil, nine surface-water and 13 groundwater samples. Overall, Kanpur Nagar yielded 49 soil, 42 groundwater and 30 surface-water samples.Hotspots included Juhi Bamburahiya, Afim Kothi, Jajmau Industrial Area, Tezab Mill Parisar, Golaghat, Panki Industrial Area and Noreya Kheda. A Sept 28 progress report stated that the institute collected 166 samples from nine hotspots in Kanpur Dehat, including 75 groundwater, 19 surface-water and 72 soil samples.IIT-Kanpur was tasked with scientifically assessing heavy-metal contamination, mapping it using Geographic Information System (GIS) technology, and recommending environmental restoration measures. UPSIDA allocated Rs 2.655 crore for the project.Initial sampling in heavily contaminated areas was completed between July and Sept. Laboratory analysis was scheduled from July to Oct, while post-monsoon air-quality assessment and GIS mapping were set to begin in Oct. Comprehensive technical recommendations were expected to be finalised from Nov.IIT-Kanpur and the district magistrates of the three districts signed a memorandum of understanding in the second week of June 2026. This followed formal communications from the respective DMs and the secretary of the UP govt’s Environment, Forest and Climate Change Division.The state govt had approved IIT-Kanpur’s proposal before the agreement was signed. The project covered groundwater, surface water, soil and air sampling, along with the identification of industrial effluent discharge points, contamination pathways, and the distribution of industrial contaminants and heavy metals.The three districts were designated environmentally sensitive because of historical industrial operations and documented pollution incidents. Earlier investigations raised concerns about contamination of water, soil and agricultural land, particularly near leather tanneries, old chromium-waste disposal sites and manufacturing facilities. articles.title: ELI STEELE: France's schools are burning. White guilt is helping fan the flames
articles.summary: A burning school in Nantes and Palestinian flags in the streets reveal how White guilt fuels France's student protests, author and filmmaker Eli Steele argues
articles.body: Editor's note: This op-ed is part of a series by Eli Steele exploring White guilt in America and the West. Steele is the director of the newly released documentary essay, "White Guilt." See the film at WhiteGuiltFilm.com. One of the most striking images of the riots that I saw sweeping France in recent days was that of a burning school in Nantes. The student movement in the streets around the school called itself a demand for education. I was scrolling through my X feed when I saw the image of a burning trash can outside Lycée Nelson Mandela. The flames spread to the walls of the building and into the glass entrance hall. There were still students in their classrooms and, thankfully, every one of them got out. When this school opened 12 years ago, its construction cost approximately €64 million, and it was touted as a beacon of hope and possibility for young people. Now the school has been shuttered for repairs, and its 1,700 students must learn from home for the time being. TRUMP, WALTZ LINK FRANCE RIOTS TO MASS IMMIGRATION AS THOUSANDS ARE ARRESTED And that is just one school. According to the education minister, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked since late September, and about 30,000 students won't see the inside of their classrooms for weeks. More than 6,500 people have been arrested, most of them minors. At least 215 students have been hurt, along with 85 teachers and staff. A 16-year-old lost the use of an eye. In La Ciotat, a physics teacher was sprayed in the face with gasoline and struck by a student from his own lycée while trying to put out a fire. Many media figures and nonprofit organizations like Amnesty International emphasized the students’ demands for better educational conditions and criticized the police response, while also acknowledging violence by some demonstrators. The demands were for more teachers, smaller classes, and decent buildings. FRENCH PM REJECTS POLICE BRUTALITY CLAIMS AFTER TEENS SEVERELY INJURED IN PROTESTS: 'ACCIDENTS HAPPEN' In the more shocking videos that flowed from the streets of France out into the world, there were teachers who made a point of standing with the students in the streets. In some cases, parents and union members joined in. The mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko, stood with students who were blockading their own school and argued that violence can sometimes be legitimate, although he also said he opposed violence and called for de-escalation. No matter what France does, it loses. Every attempt by the 'oppressor system' to restore law and order becomes a new grievance for the oppressed. As one watches the footage of students swarming the streets, seemingly with impunity, one has to wonder how the civilization that gave the world Voltaire, Rousseau, Camus and the free public school arrived at a place where schools can burn amid a movement demanding better schools. FRANCE’S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT In more ways than one, this is just an old story. A post-1960s story. What is happening in the streets of France is the latest iteration of the White guilt formula that has its roots in America. My father, Shelby Steele, has written about White guilt since the 1980s. For him, White guilt is not personal. It is not the guilt a person feels for something he did. Almost no Whites alive today owned slaves or ran colonies. How can one feel guilt for sins one did not commit? ELI STEELE: THE TERROR OF BEING CALLED RACIST IS CRUSHING FREE SPEECH IN AMERICA White guilt is collective guilt. The left has condemned all Whites for the sins of the West, from slavery and segregation to colonialism. It has made whiteness a symbol of historical evil that must be torn down. In doing so, it has created the terror of being called a racist or a colonialist and stripped of moral authority. To escape that terror, many Whites try to buy their way out. But only the "oppressed" can grant innocence, and so a bargain is struck. The "oppressed" sell victimhood for power. The "oppressor" buys innocence with deference, programs, and lower expectations, and when the pressure is high enough, silence in the face of the match. Both sides get what they want, except the children, who are mere pawns. In the 1960s, people were oppressed. Today they are taught oppression. Most of these students never lived under colonialism. They have been taught that they still do. There is a difference between then and now. In the 1960s, people were oppressed. Today they are taught oppression. Most of these students never lived under colonialism. They have been taught that they still do. So, we should not be surprised, and yet it is still startling, that one of the main features of these protests has often been the Palestinian flag. A flag about Gaza has nothing to do with class sizes in Nantes, and yet it says everything about this movement. ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA' It does two things at once. First, it is an accusation. The students have been taught that Israel is the genocidal oppressor and the Palestinians their innocent victims. When they raise that flag, they are accusing France of being like Israel. Second, it is the claim that the students are the Palestinians in this situation and therefore they are the inheritors of the victimhood that the flag symbolizes. They have granted themselves innocence and moral legitimacy through victimhood. When the Saint-Denis mayor claims that violence can be legitimate, he is merely following the script of the Black Lives Matter activists who called the 2020 looting across America reparations. If he stood against the students and demanded the Western values of responsibility and accountability, he would be branded a traitor to the cause. After all, the victims must remain victims. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The blockades have spread from the suburbs into Paris, all the way to the most elite lycées in France, and even private schools. These private school students come from comparatively privileged backgrounds and, judging from the photos of the barricades, many are White. White guilt rewards even the White students if they do one key thing: dissociate from the evil West. Their reward for allying with the oppressed is innocence. No matter what France does, it loses. Every attempt by the "oppressor system" to restore law and order becomes a new grievance for the oppressed. When one insists that a newish €64 million school is not a symbol of neglect, one is cast out with contempt as a racist. When a care worker at a Marseille bus stop told students not to smash the shelter and to go protest instead, a 15-year-old fired a flaming spray into her face. Afterward, she still called their cause "noble, legitimate." The "oppressed" will never give up the grievance, because under White guilt it is their only power. The White guilt elites only care about the innocence they gain from escaping the oppressor box via allyship. After all, they see their own nation as the oppressor. So the decline continues. It was the idea that a nation can defend itself, its laws and principles without first confessing to its past sins. White guilt makes that defense difficult, if not impossible. articles.title: Israeli settlers take Palestinian olives, and their harvest traditions
articles.summary: As Israeli settlers harvest olives on Palestinian land, farmers face growing violence and loss of an ancient tradition.
articles.body:
Ramallah, occupied West Bank – The video shared in Israeli settler groups shows two men bashing an olive tree with long wooden sticks. Smiling and congratulating one another, they try to knock the olives to the ground. They call the result “Pure Olive Oil”.

But as Palestinian activist Bashar Qaryouti explained, the two men don’t own the land, the trees, or the olives.

They’re Israeli settlers who set up an illegal settlement outpost on private property in the village of Qaryut, in the northern occupied West Bank, and made their way into this olive grove, some 200 metres (656 feet) away from Palestinian homes.

“No one has come near here for about three years, thank God,” one of the two men in the video says in Hebrew.

Local Palestinians know the man by name, and he does little to hide. The man is Avichai Suissa, an Israeli settler sanctioned by the European Union, United Kingdom – and previously by the United States – who runs a farm on the outpost. It was established more than a year and a half ago, and videos like this help Suissa raise donations for it.

On his campaign page, he says the goal is to rebuild and expand the farm, which was once dismantled by the Israeli army, to prevent it from falling “into enemy hands”.

“We’re gradually starting to work our way into the area,” Suissa said in the video.

But the land belongs to Palestinians – residents of Qaryut – who have not been able to reach it since the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023. “A few months ago, farmers tried to plough their land, but the army stopped them,” Qaryouti said.

“After we complained, the army declared the area a closed military zone a few days ago, so settlers are going to other lands, to other olives to steal,” Qaryouti explained.

Suissa and others are part of a growing movement of settlers who have intensified their campaign against the olive harvest . The campaign, part of a settler pogrom against Palestinians in the West Bank, has turned the olive harvest season in October into a source of fear and danger.

Many Palestinians in the occupied West Bank describe this year as the worst yet in terms of settler attacks, and the season has barely started.

On Wednesday, armed Israeli settlers on tractors raided lands between the villages of Ramin and Burqa, in the northern occupied West Bank. They opened fire on farmers heading to their trees.

Ali Bazzari, a 44-year-old farmer, was killed . His only “crime”, the family says, was trying to pick his olives.

Witnesses say the Israeli army prevented ambulances from reaching the wounded. Palestinians had to carry the injured through the mountains to hospitals.

The Israeli Rights Group Yesh Din says it documented 109 incidents of violence directly related to the harvest in 75 Palestinian communities between September 27 and October 6, an average of 11 per day.

Israeli settlers are increasingly attempting to adopt the rituals of the olive harvest season , while pushing out the Palestinians who have kept those traditions for generations.

Several new farms have been set up in the occupied West Bank. One shares videos of olives being pressed. Others invite Israelis to “join in” the experience.

Palestinians say the videos circulating show a disregard for the actual owners of the land taken by the settlers, and a clear attempt to appropriate the season, imitating its rituals and claiming them as their own.

Those rituals – things like collective picking, singing, and shared meals on the farms – are rooted in a deep connection to the land.

The olive harvest season may be an exhausting time of the year for Palestinians, with its hard work and long hours in the sun, but it’s a rewarding one. Olive farmers traditionally gather for family get-togethers, with neighbours and friends volunteering to help one another harvest the olives, in a cultural tradition known as “ouneh”.

The season has a light-hearted element, with debates about whose land produces the best oil, who should charge the most, and who knows how to pick the most olives and not drop any to the ground.

Older generations pass down lessons from history, such as the best time to harvest and how to nurture the trees – an inherited knowledge of climate, agriculture and the land itself.

“They planted so that we can eat. We plant so they [will] eat,” a well-known Arabic saying goes. It highlights the continuity of this inheritance, and the responsibility towards future generations.

These trees, which are meant to be protected, nurtured and passed on, are being taken away – not only by settlers, but by soldiers, too.

Hazem Sanaf, 61, stood on a nearby hill in the village of Beit Rima and watched as Israeli bulldozers ploughed through his lands in late September, after he had received an Israeli military order. The bulldozers destroyed and uprooted more than 400 trees belonging to Hazem and his neighbour, some of them decades old, and his only source of income.

“They just want to take our olive trees from us,” he said, his eyes reflecting his pain.

Hazem is not alone. Several Israeli military orders to uproot olive trees have been handed out across the occupied West Bank. Some have been carried out, while others await their turn.

In the past, the Israeli military has cited the need to clear land of trees to prevent security threats or ambushes on troops. But Palestinians say it reflects a pattern of dispossession and impoverishment.

According to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission (CRRC), Israeli settlers and soldiers have destroyed approximately 50,000 trees this year alone.

Fuad Daraghmeh, from the village of al-Lubban Asharqiya, near Ramallah, carried the thick, broken stem of a tree.

“I took care of it for 30 years,” he said, and headed home. He did not say what he planned to do with the stem, but others said that their trees had been uprooted before, and that they had managed to nourish them back to life.

Others are resigned to saying goodbye to the trees. They sit by the bulldozed trees with small hand tools, picking the last fruit of what they believe is their last crop.

Palestinians have been watching videos of settlers harvesting their olive trees, including the one shared by Suissa.

Beyond the pain, one remark keeps coming up: the method used by Suissa in vigorously beating the tree is no way to treat it, and no way to harvest olives.

“The people who have tended to their lands for decades know that,” one Palestinian activist, who did not wish to be identified for security reasons, said.
